note: AI-written explanations for pooled questions published without one (scripts/explain-mcq.mjs, lib/mcq-explain.mjs). Each was reviewed by a second call and kept only when accurate and consistent with the key; hash ties it to the question as it is. refused: the last refusal per question.

headqa-2013-101.why: Mild hypercalcaemia with an inappropriately normal PTH, a family history, and relatives who stayed hypercalcaemic after parathyroid surgery points to familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia. Low urinary calcium excretion confirms it: a calcium/creatinine clearance ratio below 0.01.
notes: 25-OH vitamin D shows vitamin D stores. It does not tell FHH apart from primary hyperparathyroidism, which is the key question here.
1,25-(OH)2 vitamin D can be high or normal in both PTH-mediated states and in granulomatous disease. It does not separate FHH from primary hyperparathyroidism.
Tubular phosphate reabsorption falls under PTH action in both conditions, so it does not tell them apart. Urinary calcium excretion is what separates them.
PTHrP is used for humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy, where PTH is suppressed. Here PTH is not suppressed and the patient is a healthy 30-year-old with a family history.

headqa-2013-106.why: Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (schistocytes, high LDH, high reticulocytes, raised bilirubin) plus severe thrombocytopenia and normal clotting tests means TTP. Ticlopidine is a classic cause of TTP. Remember that clotting tests are normal in TTP and abnormal in DIC.
notes: Immune thrombocytopenia causes isolated thrombocytopenia. It does not cause schistocytes, haemolysis or a very high LDH.
Aplastic anaemia causes pancytopenia with low reticulocytes. Here the white count is normal and reticulocytes are high, which shows peripheral destruction.
Simple drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia lowers platelets only. The schistocytic haemolytic anaemia points to ticlopidine-associated TTP.
DIC would prolong the APTT and PT and consume fibrinogen. All of these are normal here.

headqa-2013-108.why: A young woman after a viral illness with isolated, confirmed severe thrombocytopenia, a normal smear and no organomegaly has primary immune thrombocytopenia. First-line treatment is corticosteroids. The intended dose is prednisone 1 mg/kg/day ("1 mg/day" is a typo); in Australia prednisolone is used.
notes: Transfused platelets are destroyed quickly in ITP. Transfusion is kept for life-threatening bleeding, alongside steroids and IVIG, and this patient is stable with only skin bleeding.
Rituximab is a second-line option for ITP that persists or comes back after steroids. It is not the first treatment.
Cyclophosphamide is a later-line immunosuppressant for refractory ITP and is never used first.
Plasma exchange treats TTP. There are no schistocytes and LDH is normal, so TTP is excluded.

headqa-2013-110.why: A painless chancre with inguinal nodes two months ago, followed by fever and malaise with high-titre RPR and TPHA, is early (secondary) syphilis. A single dose of benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM is curative. In Australia this is Bicillin L-A 1.8 g (2.4 MU) IM once.
notes: Reactive treponemal and non-treponemal tests with a high RPR titre mean active syphilis, which must be treated. Partners also need tracing.
High-dose IV penicillin G for 10 to 14 days is for neurosyphilis or ocular syphilis. There are no neurological or eye features here.
Three weekly doses are for late latent syphilis, latent syphilis of unknown duration, or tertiary syphilis. This infection began within the last few months.
A single dose of ceftriaxone treats gonorrhoea, not syphilis. Ceftriaxone is only an alternative for syphilis, given as repeated doses.

headqa-2013-112.why: Sudden high fever with myalgia and headache in a returning traveller, then a maculopapular rash turning petechial around day 3 to 5, with leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and mildly raised transaminases, after malaria has been excluded, is classic dengue.
notes: Coronavirus infections mainly cause respiratory illness. They do not give a petechial rash with leukopenia and thrombocytopenia after travel.
Lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus spreads from rodents and causes a febrile illness with aseptic meningitis. It does not cause a haemorrhagic rash or thrombocytopenia.
Chikungunya looks similar, but its hallmark is severe and often lasting polyarthralgia or arthritis. Marked thrombocytopenia and petechiae favour dengue.
St Louis encephalitis is a flavivirus infection that causes encephalitis in older adults. There is no altered consciousness here, and it does not cause a petechial rash.

headqa-2013-116.why: Fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes and no cough give a full Centor score, so group A streptococcal pharyngitis is likely. Narrow-spectrum penicillin V or amoxicillin for 10 days is the treatment of choice. Australian guidelines also use phenoxymethylpenicillin for 10 days.
notes: GAS is always sensitive to penicillin. Adding clavulanate only widens the spectrum and raises side effects with no benefit.
Doxycycline is unreliable against group A streptococcus and is not used for streptococcal pharyngitis.
Ciprofloxacin has poor activity against streptococci and is not suitable for tonsillitis.
Metronidazole covers anaerobes and protozoa, not group A streptococcus.

headqa-2013-126.why: Pulmonary haemorrhage, rapidly progressive renal failure with crescents, high-titre anti-GBM antibodies and linear IgG deposits mean anti-GBM (Goodpasture) disease. Treatment is plasma exchange plus corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide. Pulmonary haemorrhage is an indication for plasma exchange whatever the renal prognosis.
notes: IgA nephropathy shows mesangial granular IgA deposits and anti-GBM is negative. Here immunofluorescence is linear and anti-GBM is strongly positive.
Membranous nephropathy causes nephrotic syndrome with subepithelial granular IgG deposits. It does not cause crescentic failure with hemoptysis and linear staining.
Mycophenolate is not induction therapy for anti-GBM disease. The standard is plasma exchange, steroids and cyclophosphamide.
The linear pattern shows antibodies binding directly to the basement membrane (type II hypersensitivity). Immune complexes give a granular pattern.

headqa-2013-130.why: A young man with a testicular mass, very high beta-hCG and multiple cannonball lung metastases with early blood-borne spread most likely has choriocarcinoma. It is a trophoblastic germ cell tumour that makes large amounts of hCG and spreads early through the blood.
notes: Seminoma can raise beta-hCG only modestly, through syncytiotrophoblast cells. It usually spreads to retroperitoneal nodes first, not to many lung nodules with hCG this high.
Renal angiomyolipoma is a benign tumour linked with tuberous sclerosis. It does not cause a testicular mass, hCG elevation or lung metastases.
Wilms tumour is a kidney tumour of young children. It is not a testicular cancer in a 26-year-old and does not make hCG.
Testicular lymphoma affects older men, usually over 60, and does not produce beta-hCG.

headqa-2013-131.why: A PSA of 5.9 ng/mL with a low free/total ratio (11%), a firm right lobe on DRE and a father with prostate cancer make cancer likely, and only a biopsy can confirm it. In Australia, multiparametric MRI usually comes first to target the biopsy, often done by the transperineal route.
notes: Abdominopelvic CT is for staging and is only considered after a biopsy confirms cancer. Even then it is reserved for higher-risk disease, so it is premature here.
5-alpha reductase inhibitors lower PSA and would hide a likely cancer. They are a treatment for benign prostatic hyperplasia, not a response to a suspicious DRE.
Androgen deprivation is for confirmed, usually advanced or high-risk, prostate cancer. It is never started without a tissue diagnosis.
A bone scan stages confirmed high-risk disease. It is not indicated before histology, and an asymptomatic man with a PSA under 10 has a low chance of bone metastases.

headqa-2013-133.why: This is a severe exacerbation: RR 42, accessory muscle use, PaO2 54 on 28% O2. A normal pCO2 in a tachypnoeic asthmatic means he is tiring. NIV has weak evidence in asthma and can delay intubation, so it is the least indicated step. The Australian Asthma Handbook likewise does not recommend routine NIV.
notes: He is hypoxaemic at 54 mmHg on 28% oxygen, so titrating oxygen up to an adequate saturation is clearly indicated (Australian target SpO2 93-95%).
Early systemic corticosteroids are standard in any moderate-severe exacerbation; IV methylprednisolone is appropriate, though Australian practice often uses IV hydrocortisone or oral prednisolone.
Adding ipratropium to repeated salbutamol nebulisation improves outcomes in severe exacerbations and is recommended when there is a poor response to beta-agonist alone.
IV magnesium sulfate is recommended for severe or life-threatening asthma that does not respond to initial bronchodilators, as in this patient.

headqa-2013-142.why: Pain and swelling of the whole leg from the groin in a patient with active cancer on chemotherapy gives a high pretest probability of proximal DVT. Venous compression Doppler ultrasound is accurate, non-invasive and cheap, so it is the most cost-effective confirmatory test.
notes: D-dimer only helps to exclude DVT when probability is low and is often raised in cancer, so it cannot confirm the diagnosis in this high-probability patient.
MR venography is accurate but expensive and less available. It is reserved for pelvic or iliac clots that ultrasound cannot show.
Contrast phlebography is the historical gold standard but is invasive and needs contrast, so it is not cost-effective as first-line confirmation.
CT venography adds radiation, contrast and cost, and it is not the first-line test for suspected lower-limb DVT.

headqa-2013-147.why: Coma after high-speed acceleration-deceleration trauma that does not match the initial CT, plus small punctate haemorrhages in the corpus callosum and at the grey-white junction, is typical of diffuse axonal injury. Corpus callosum involvement means severe (higher grade) injury.
notes: An acute subdural haematoma shows on CT as a crescent-shaped extra-axial collection, not as punctate lesions deep in the white matter.
TTP is a haematological disorder with thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic haemolysis, and it does not explain traumatic coma with this CT pattern.
Haemorrhagic contusions are focal cortical lesions, typically frontal and temporal poles (coup-contrecoup). They do not involve the corpus callosum.
Hypoxic-ischaemic injury affects watershed cortex, basal ganglia and hippocampi diffusely after hypoxia or arrest. It does not produce punctate callosal haemorrhages.

headqa-2013-149.why: Dementia with early parkinsonism and visual hallucinations, then marked motor worsening on a low-dose antipsychotic, is classic dementia with Lewy bodies. Severe sensitivity to neuroleptics is a supportive feature, so avoid typical antipsychotics and use even risperidone with great caution.
notes: Alzheimer disease begins with memory loss, and early parkinsonism, early hallucinations and severe neuroleptic sensitivity are not typical of it.
Frontotemporal dementia presents with behavioural or language change, and prominent visual hallucinations with early parkinsonism are not typical of it.
Vascular dementia usually progresses stepwise with focal signs and vascular risk factors, and severe neuroleptic sensitivity is not one of its features.
Sporadic CJD progresses over weeks with myoclonus and ataxia. Eight months of slow decline with neuroleptic sensitivity fits Lewy body disease much better.

headqa-2013-152.why: A lobar (cortico-subcortical) haemorrhage in an 80-year-old with progressive cognitive impairment strongly suggests cerebral amyloid angiopathy. Remember: hypertension causes deep bleeds (basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, cerebellum), while amyloid angiopathy causes lobar bleeds in the elderly.
notes: AVMs cause lobar haemorrhage mainly in young patients. They would not explain an 80-year-old's background cognitive decline.
Hypertensive haemorrhages are typically deep, and this patient's blood pressure is well controlled, so a lobar bleed points elsewhere.
Isolated CNS vasculitis is rare and presents with headache, multifocal ischaemic events and encephalopathy rather than a single lobar haematoma.
A bleeding tumour is possible, but the absence of contrast enhancement and the history of cognitive decline favour amyloid angiopathy.

headqa-2013-160.why: An older patient with back pain, leg weakness and paraesthesia that come on after walking a short distance (neurogenic claudication), and who leans forward for relief because flexion widens the canal, has lumbar spinal canal stenosis.
notes: An osteoporotic vertebral fracture causes sudden localised back pain, often after minor strain. It does not cause walking-related leg symptoms relieved by flexion.
A central L5-S1 herniation is acute, with radicular pain or cauda equina features. It is not a gradual walking-induced claudication relieved by leaning forward.
Spondylodiscitis causes constant, inflammatory, night-time back pain with fever or raised inflammatory markers, not neurogenic claudication.
Degenerative scoliosis can coexist with stenosis and cause back pain, but the claudication pattern relieved by forward flexion is the hallmark of canal stenosis itself.

headqa-2013-169.why: Thick, yellowish, gelatinous fluid that is hard to aspirate is mucinous ascites (pseudomyxoma peritonei). This comes from a mucin-producing adenocarcinoma, usually appendiceal or ovarian, spreading through the peritoneum. Small implants are often missed on imaging. Remember: gelatinous ascites means mucinous adenocarcinoma.
notes: Cirrhotic ascites is thin, clear and straw-coloured, and the liver and spleen are normal on imaging here, so there is no sign of portal hypertension.
Chylous ascites is milky white and high in triglycerides, not gelatinous, and imaging shows no lymphadenopathy or masses to suggest lymphoma.
Tuberculous ascites is a clear or turbid exudate high in lymphocytes and ADA, often with fever. It is not thick, mucoid fluid that is hard to aspirate.
Constrictive pericarditis gives thin, high-protein ascites (SAAG of 1.1 or more) with a raised JVP and hepatic congestion, and none of these fits gelatinous fluid with a normal liver.

headqa-2013-175.why: Mild dehydration from viral gastroenteritis in a child who tolerates fluids is treated with a low-osmolality oral rehydration solution and early return to the usual diet. Early feeding shortens the illness and improves nutrition. Australian guidelines say the same, using ORS products such as Gastrolyte.
notes: IV fluids are for severe dehydration or when oral or nasogastric rehydration fails, and fasting and restrictive astringent diets are outdated and not helpful.
Antibiotics are not indicated for presumed viral gastroenteritis without blood or mucus in an otherwise healthy child.
Lactose-free formula is not needed routinely. Consider it only if diarrhoea persists with proven secondary lactose intolerance.
Loperamide is contraindicated in young children because of the risk of ileus and CNS toxicity, and it does not treat the dehydration.

headqa-2013-180.why: Allergen exposure followed by skin and mucosal signs plus airway involvement (hoarseness, wheeze, SpO2 93%) and hypotension is anaphylaxis. First-line treatment is 1:1000 adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg IM into the anterolateral thigh, as ASCIA guidelines also recommend.
notes: Inducing vomiting is not recommended. It delays adrenaline and risks aspiration in a child with airway compromise.
Subcutaneous adrenaline is absorbed more slowly and less reliably than IM, so it is no longer advised for anaphylaxis.
Corticosteroids work too slowly to treat acute anaphylaxis and do not replace adrenaline. At most they are an adjunct.
Nebulised salbutamol can help residual bronchospasm after adrenaline, but it does nothing for the hypotension or the upper airway oedema.

headqa-2013-184.why: Repeated painless second-trimester losses with advanced dilation and bulging membranes, and no contractions, after a conization point to cervical insufficiency. A history-indicated cerclage at about 12-14 weeks is the recommended prevention.
notes: Atosiban is an IV tocolytic for active preterm labour. It is not given orally and is not used as prophylaxis, and these losses happened without contractions.
Steroids at 19-20 weeks come before viability and would not prevent painless cervical dilation, so they would not save the pregnancy.
Cervical insufficiency can be treated and cerclage gives good outcomes, so advising against further pregnancy is inappropriate.
She has no fertility problem, since she conceives easily. Her problem is keeping the pregnancy, so assisted reproduction adds nothing.

headqa-2013-188.why: Primary amenorrhoea with normal female secondary sexual characteristics, normal ovaries and hormones, an absent vagina and uterus, and unilateral renal agenesis is Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome. It is Müllerian agenesis in a 46,XX female, and renal anomalies often go with it.
notes: Androgen insensitivity (Morris syndrome) gives a blind vagina and no uterus, but there are testes instead of ovaries, testosterone is in the male range, and pubic hair is scant.
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia causes virilisation and high androgens, and the uterus and vagina are present.
PCOS causes oligo-amenorrhoea with hyperandrogenism, and the uterus and vagina are normal.
Kallmann syndrome is hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia, so oestradiol is low, puberty is absent, and the uterus is present.

headqa-2013-220.why: She has well over five depressive symptoms (low mood, anhedonia, guilt, weight loss, early waking, low energy, poor concentration) lasting more than two weeks with marked impairment. That meets major depressive episode criteria. A recent stressor does not change the diagnosis once full criteria are met.
notes: Dysthymia needs chronic, milder symptoms lasting at least two years, not one month of severe symptoms.
Pseudodementia is cognitive impairment caused by depression. Memory loss here is one symptom inside a full depressive syndrome, which is the main diagnosis.
Adjustment disorder applies only when symptoms after a stressor do not meet criteria for another disorder such as major depression.
Minor depression means fewer than five symptoms, but she has many more, with severe functional impairment.

headqa-2013-233.why: A tall person with a female phenotype, good breast development, scant pubic and axillary hair, primary amenorrhoea and high gonadotropins has complete androgen insensitivity (46,XY). Testes make testosterone, which is converted to oestradiol and drives breast growth. Androgen-dependent hair does not develop because the androgen receptor does not work.
notes: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) gives a male phenotype with small testes and gynaecomastia, not female external genitalia and primary amenorrhoea.
Kallmann syndrome is hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia, so gonadotropins would be low and breast development absent or poor.
Constitutional delay gives low gonadotropins and a delayed bone age with little pubertal development. Here bone age matches chronological age and gonadotropins are high.
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia in a 46,XX patient causes virilisation with abundant androgen-dependent hair and short adult height, the opposite of scant hair and tall stature.

headqa-2013-42.why: ACE inhibitors such as enalapril cause a dry, tickly cough because bradykinin builds up, and they cause hyperkalaemia because they reduce aldosterone. Cough plus high potassium in a patient with hypertension and heart failure points to this class.
notes: Thiazides cause hypokalaemia, not hyperkalaemia, and do not cause cough.
Beta-blockers may cause bronchospasm in susceptible people but not a dry tickly cough, and they do not typically cause clinically important hyperkalaemia.
Loop diuretics such as furosemide cause hypokalaemia and do not cause cough.
Hydralazine causes reflex tachycardia, headache and a lupus-like syndrome, not cough or hyperkalaemia.

headqa-2013-64.why: A wide, fixed split second heart sound is the hallmark of atrial septal defect. Add a pulmonary flow murmur, right axis deviation, RBBB, and adult-onset AF with right heart failure, and this is a secundum ASD presenting in middle age.
notes: VSD gives a holosystolic murmur at the left sternal border, and fixed splitting of the second sound is not typical.
Aortic stenosis gives an ejection murmur at the aortic area radiating to the carotids, with a soft or paradoxically split second sound and left ventricular hypertrophy on ECG.
Mitral stenosis causes AF but gives a diastolic rumble with an opening snap at the apex, not fixed splitting.
A patent ductus gives a continuous machinery murmur below the left clavicle and wide pulse pressure, not fixed splitting of the second sound.

headqa-2013-68.why: Mean gradient over 40 mmHg and valve area under 1 cm2 mean severe aortic stenosis, and exertional dyspnoea means it is symptomatic. Severe symptomatic AS needs valve replacement whatever the EF. At 52 with no high-risk features, surgical AVR is standard, and Australian practice is the same.
notes: Medical therapy does not change the prognosis of severe symptomatic AS, and diuretics can drop preload dangerously; delaying intervention once symptoms start increases mortality.
Balloon valvuloplasty gives only short-lived benefit with early restenosis, so it is used as a bridge or palliation, not as definitive treatment for a fit 52-year-old.
Homografts are mainly used in special cases such as aortic root endocarditis; they are not the standard replacement for isolated degenerative or calcific AS.
TAVI is used mainly in older or higher surgical-risk patients; a fit 52-year-old is better treated with surgical AVR, given long-term durability.

headqa-2013-78.why: Symptoms within 30 minutes of eating after vagotomy and Billroth II are early dumping syndrome, caused by rapid hyperosmolar emptying into the jejunum. First-line treatment is diet: small frequent meals, few simple sugars, liquids taken apart from solids, and lying down after meals.
notes: Octreotide works but is kept for dumping that does not respond to dietary changes, not used as first-line.
Benzodiazepines do nothing for the physiology of dumping; the symptoms come from fluid shifts and vasoactive peptides, not anxiety.
The timing just after gastric surgery and the link to meals clearly point to dumping, so searching for a carcinoid or other NET is not justified.
Revision to a Roux-en-Y is only for severe dumping that has failed both diet and drug treatment, not for initial management at six weeks.

headqa-2013-82.why: Negative HLA-DQ2 and DQ8 almost rules out coeliac disease because the negative predictive value is close to 100%. In a 55-year-old, iron deficiency anaemia with a new change in bowel habit points to colorectal cancer, so colonoscopy is the test. In Australian practice, bidirectional endoscopy (gastroscopy plus colonoscopy) is usual for iron deficiency anaemia.
notes: Coeliac serology adds nothing once HLA-DQ2 and DQ8 are negative, because coeliac disease is then almost excluded.
Duodenal biopsy for coeliac disease is not justified after negative HLA typing, and on its own it would miss the colorectal cancer suggested by anaemia plus a change in bowel habit.
The D-xylose test is an outdated screen for malabsorption and cannot assess for colorectal neoplasia.
A gluten-free diet trial is not a valid diagnostic test, and it would delay investigation of a likely colorectal cancer.

headqa-2013-90.why: Heavy drinking that recently increased, followed by fever, painful hepatomegaly, marked jaundice, neutrophilia, an AST:ALT ratio above 2 with AST under 400, very high GGT, macrocytosis, coagulopathy and encephalopathy, is severe alcoholic hepatitis. Assess severity with the Maddrey discriminant function (severe if 32 or more) or MELD.
notes: A liver abscess causes fever and right upper quadrant pain, but deep jaundice, encephalopathy, coagulopathy and an alcoholic AST:ALT pattern point to diffuse hepatocellular injury, not a focal lesion.
Acute cholecystitis gives right upper quadrant pain with a Murphy sign, and usually no or only mild jaundice. It does not cause encephalopathy, coagulopathy or macrocytosis.
Cholangitis gives fever, jaundice and pain with a cholestatic pattern from biliary obstruction. The alcohol history, AST:ALT above 2 and liver failure point to alcoholic hepatitis.
Acute pancreatitis presents with epigastric pain radiating to the back and raised lipase. It would not explain painful hepatomegaly, bilirubin of 15 mg/dL and liver failure.

headqa-2013-91.why: A healthy young man has episodic jaundice with isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, normal liver enzymes, no anaemia (so no haemolysis) and a normal liver on ultrasound. This is Gilbert syndrome, caused by reduced UGT1A1 activity. Episodes are often brought on by fasting, exercise or illness.
notes: Rotor syndrome causes conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinaemia, but here direct bilirubin is only 0.4 of 3.2 mg/dL.
Choledocholithiasis causes conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with raised ALP and GGT, a dilated bile duct and often pain, and none of these is present.
Dubin-Johnson syndrome is a conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, whereas this patient's raised bilirubin is mostly unconjugated.
Acute hepatitis would raise ALT and AST, usually markedly, along with mixed hyperbilirubinaemia. Here the transaminases are normal.

headqa-2013-99.why: A pancreatic NET, recurrent kidney stones from a young age (primary hyperparathyroidism), amenorrhoea (likely prolactinoma) and a family history of stones make the 3 Ps of MEN1: parathyroid, pancreas and pituitary.
notes: MEN2A combines medullary thyroid cancer, phaeochromocytoma and hyperparathyroidism; it does not include pancreatic NETs or pituitary tumours.
MEN2B causes medullary thyroid cancer, phaeochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas and a marfanoid build, but not hyperparathyroidism or pancreatic NETs.
Somatostatinoma causes gallstones, diabetes and steatorrhoea; it does not explain lifelong kidney stones, amenorrhoea or the family history.
An ectopic PTH-secreting NET is very rare and would not explain stones since age 20, the family history of stones or the amenorrhoea.

headqa-2014-106.why: Renal failure that develops weeks after arterial catheterisation, together with blue or purple toes and worsening hypertension, points to cholesterol atheroembolism. Look for supporting signs such as eosinophilia, eosinophiluria and low complement. Renal function usually declines slowly over weeks and often does not recover.
notes: Malignant hypertension needs retinopathy (papilloedema, haemorrhages) and usually microangiopathic haemolysis, and it does not explain purple toe lesions after catheterisation.
Contrast nephropathy starts within 24 to 72 hours of contrast and usually recovers, so it does not fit renal failure appearing 3 weeks later with toe lesions.
Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis presents with nephritic sediment and is not linked to a recent vascular procedure or to purple toe lesions.
Bilateral renal artery stenosis can cause hypertension and renal impairment, but it does not cause distal embolic skin lesions in the feet after catheterisation.

headqa-2014-110.why: Long-standing uncontrolled RA with a very high CRP, nephrotic-range proteinuria, and a thick-walled restrictive heart with conduction disease point to one systemic infiltrative process: secondary AA amyloidosis.
notes: Cardiorenal syndrome type 2 is CKD caused by chronic heart failure; it does not explain nephrotic proteinuria or a thick-walled restrictive ventricle.
Giant cell myocarditis is a fulminant illness of younger patients with ventricular arrhythmias; it does not cause a restrictive thick-walled picture with nephrotic syndrome.
Anti-TNF drugs can worsen heart failure, but they do not cause wall thickening, restrictive filling or nephrotic proteinuria.
Membranous nephropathy in RA, usually from gold or penicillamine, could explain the proteinuria but not the restrictive infiltrative cardiomyopathy.

headqa-2014-115.why: This is stage I sarcoidosis (bilateral hilar lymph nodes, noncaseating granulomas, raised ACE) with mild skin lesions and no symptoms. It often resolves on its own, so treatment is not needed yet. Workup should continue: lung function tests, eye exam, ECG, and serum and urine calcium.
notes: Oral corticosteroids are kept for symptomatic or progressive lung disease, or for heart, eye, nerve or high-calcium involvement, none of which is present.
Hydroxychloroquine can treat troublesome skin sarcoid, but these minor symptom-free lesions do not need systemic therapy.
Azathioprine is a second-line steroid-sparing drug for chronic disease that needs treatment, not for symptom-free stage I sarcoidosis.
Leflunomide is a second-line steroid-sparing drug kept for refractory or steroid-dependent sarcoidosis, which is not the case here.

headqa-2014-119.why: A twisting injury with a pop, instability, rapid bloody effusion and a positive Lachman test means ACL rupture. No fat droplets in the aspirated blood argues against a fracture. The ACL is the most common cause of acute traumatic haemarthrosis.
notes: A bucket-handle meniscal tear typically causes mechanical locking and a block to extension, but knee movement here is free and Lachman is positive.
The LCL lies outside the joint, so an isolated tear causes varus laxity without a large haemarthrosis or a positive Lachman.
A tibial spine avulsion is a bone injury, so fat droplets would appear in the haemarthrosis, and it is mostly seen in children.
A condylar fracture is usually high-energy and gives a haemarthrosis with fat droplets, which were absent.

headqa-2014-124.why: This is pneumococcal pneumonia with hypoxaemia (SpO2 80%) needing admission, and ceftriaxone reliably covers Streptococcus pneumoniae, including strains with reduced penicillin sensitivity. In Australia, eTG uses benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline for moderate CAP, and ceftriaxone plus azithromycin for severe CAP.
notes: Ceftazidime has weak activity against pneumococcus. It is an antipseudomonal drug and not a choice for typical CAP.
Pneumococcal macrolide resistance is high, so a macrolide alone is inadequate for a hypoxaemic inpatient.
Azithromycin alone carries the same pneumococcal resistance problem and is not enough for hospitalised pneumonia with severe hypoxaemia.
Doxycycline alone suits mild outpatient CAP, not a hypoxaemic patient needing admission with confirmed pneumococcus.

headqa-2014-146.why: Proximal muscle weakness, a heliotrope (purple) rash around the eyes and Gottron papules mean dermatomyositis. In an older adult it is strongly linked to cancer, especially ovarian, lung and GI, so a malignancy screen is mandatory.
notes: Palpable purpura on the legs and buttocks with joint and abdominal pain in a child is IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein), which is not paraneoplastic.
Target lesions with oral erosions are erythema multiforme, usually triggered by HSV or drugs, not by cancer.
A malar rash, photosensitivity and fingertip erythema point to systemic lupus, an autoimmune disease without a strong cancer link.
Symmetrical depigmented patches with patchy hair loss and broken hairs are vitiligo with alopecia areata, autoimmune conditions not linked to cancer.

headqa-2014-158.why: One first-degree relative with ovarian cancer at 64 and no other family history means only modestly raised risk, with no indication for surgery. Combined oral contraceptives cut ovarian cancer risk by about half with long-term use, and they are reversible.
notes: Tubal occlusion does lower ovarian cancer risk, but permanent sterilisation is inappropriate for a 28-year-old woman with no children.
Risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy is for proven BRCA or Lynch carriers once childbearing is complete, not for one late-onset case in the family.
Evidence that aspirin reduces ovarian cancer risk is weak and inconsistent, so it is not the recommended strategy.
Breastfeeding lowers ovarian cancer risk, so advising formula feeding would remove a protective factor rather than reduce risk.

headqa-2014-162.why: This is preterm prelabour rupture of membranes at 31 weeks, with no fever, no contractions and a normal CTG. Manage expectantly: corticosteroids for fetal lung maturation and antibiotics to prolong latency. Tocolysis is pointless when there are no contractions. In Australia this means betamethasone plus erythromycin.
notes: Tocolytics are not indicated because there are no contractions, and in PPROM they add no benefit while possibly masking infection.
Tocolysis has no role without contractions, and leaving out corticosteroids at 31 weeks forgoes the main proven fetal benefit.
Tocolytics are not needed without contractions, and leaving out antibiotics loses the latency and infection benefit shown in PPROM.
Induction with oxytocin is for PPROM near term (around 34 weeks or later) or for chorioamnionitis or fetal compromise, and none of these is present at 31 weeks.

headqa-2014-163.why: With a positive test, pain and spotting at 7 weeks, the first priority is to find where the pregnancy is and whether it is viable. Transvaginal ultrasound, usually alongside a quantitative beta-hCG, tells an intrauterine pregnancy (threatened, incomplete or missed miscarriage) apart from an ectopic before any treatment is chosen.
notes: Sending her home to rest and repeat the test in a week risks missing an ectopic pregnancy that could rupture, and rest does not change the course of a miscarriage.
Uterine evacuation before ultrasound could end a viable pregnancy and would miss an ectopic, so the diagnosis has to come first.
Progesterone could only be considered once ultrasound confirms a viable intrauterine pregnancy, and it is not the first step.
Medical evacuation with prostaglandins needs a confirmed nonviable intrauterine pregnancy, and giving it blind could harm a viable pregnancy or miss an ectopic.

headqa-2014-181.why: Risk in smokers is 30/1000 (3%) and in non-smokers 20/2000 (1%). Relative risk is 3%/1% = 3. Attributable risk is the risk difference, 3% − 1% = 2%, or 20 per 1000. Always divide events by each group's own denominator before you compare.
notes: The relative risk of 3 is right, but 10 per 1000 is the non-smokers' risk (20/2000), not the difference between the groups.
A relative risk of 1.5 comes from comparing raw counts (30 vs 20) without dividing by the unequal group sizes of 1000 and 2000.
This repeats the 1.5 error from raw counts and also gives the smokers' total risk (30/1000) instead of the excess risk.
This swaps the two measures: relative risk is a ratio with no units, and attributable risk is a rate difference.

headqa-2014-183.why: Subjects were chosen by outcome: patients with UGIB (cases) and matched patients without it (controls). Their past NSAID exposure was then compared, which is the definition of a case-control study. The usual effect measure is the odds ratio.
notes: A cohort study picks people by exposure (NSAID users and non-users) and follows them for the outcome, but here people were picked because they had or did not have bleeding.
A cross-sectional study measures exposure and outcome at one point in time in a population sample, without choosing people by outcome or matching controls.
An experimental study needs the investigator to assign NSAID exposure, which did not happen here because exposure was observed retrospectively.
An ecological study compares groups or populations rather than individuals, but here exposure and outcome were recorded for individual patients.

headqa-2014-189.why: Cases: 20 exposed and 100 unexposed. Controls: 20 exposed and 400 unexposed. OR = (20×400)/(100×20) = 4. The same number of exposed people in each group does not mean OR = 1, because the groups are different sizes.
notes: OR = 1 is the trap of comparing only the equal exposed counts (20 and 20) and ignoring that the groups have 120 and 420 people.
OR = 2 does not come from the 2×2 table. The correct cross-product is (20×400)/(100×20) = 4.
OR = 6 does not match the data. The odds of exposure are 20/100 in cases and 20/400 in controls, a ratio of 4.
OR = 8 overestimates the association. The cross-product ratio of this table is 4.

headqa-2014-197.why: Both registries contain only vaccinated people, with no unvaccinated comparison group, so only descriptive measures are possible. Hospital discharge diagnoses capture AMI, an event that leads to admission, so incidence in vaccinees can be estimated.
notes: A cohort study testing whether vaccination raises GBS risk needs an unvaccinated comparison group, and these registries contain only vaccinated people.
Fever after vaccination rarely leads to hospital admission, so discharge records would miss most cases and the incidence could not be estimated.
A clinical trial needs investigator-assigned (randomised) exposure. Existing registry data can only support observational studies.
A case-control study of vaccination as a risk factor needs controls and unvaccinated people, and neither is in these sources.

headqa-2014-198.why: NNH is the reciprocal of the absolute risk increase: 1/(0.03 - 0.01) = 1/0.02 = 50. So 50 patients must be treated for one extra severe haemorrhage attributable to the anticoagulant. Remember that NNT and NNH are always 1 divided by an absolute risk difference.
notes: The NNH is not a count of bleeding cases. The treated group had an incidence of 3%, not 50 cases.
The NNH is not an absolute excess of cases. The excess risk was 2 percentage points, not 50 extra cases.
The relative risk is 3%/1% = 3, not 50. NNH is based on absolute difference, not relative risk.
An incidence of 3% means 3 per 100 treated patients bled, not 50 per 100.

headqa-2014-228.why: She had sudden syncope, then dyspnoea, tachycardia, tachypnoea, hypotension and marked hypoxaemia (saturation 85%), yet her lungs are clear and there are no murmurs or gallop. Hypoxic shock with clear lungs points to massive (high-risk) pulmonary embolism.
notes: A posterior circulation stroke would cause neurological deficits. It would not explain severe hypoxaemia, tachypnoea and shock with clear lungs.
An acute coronary syndrome severe enough to cause shock would usually cause chest pain and pulmonary congestion or a gallop. None of these is present.
Hypovolaemic shock would not cause marked hypoxaemia and tachypnoea with clear lungs, and there is no source of fluid or blood loss.
Acute pulmonary oedema would cause crackles on auscultation, and her lungs are clear.

headqa-2014-229.why: She has a pulmonary-renal syndrome: alveolar haemorrhage with haemosiderophages, plus rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with red cell casts. Positive p-ANCA (MPO) with negative anti-GBM and ANA points to microscopic polyangiitis, a small-vessel vasculitis with pauci-immune necrotising glomerulonephritis.
notes: Idiopathic pulmonary haemosiderosis mainly affects children, does not involve the kidneys and is ANCA negative.
Goodpasture syndrome causes a pulmonary-renal picture but needs positive anti-GBM antibodies, which are negative here.
Lupus nephritis with lung haemorrhage would almost always come with positive ANA, which is negative here.
Classical polyarteritis nodosa affects medium-sized arteries, spares the lungs and glomeruli, and is typically ANCA negative.

headqa-2014-36.why: A hard, tender groin mass below the inguinal ligament with vomiting in an elderly woman suggests an incarcerated femoral hernia. Femoral hernias lie below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, are most common in older women, and often strangulate because the femoral ring is narrow.
notes: A direct inguinal hernia lies above the inguinal ligament, in Hesselbach's triangle, and rarely incarcerates.
A Spigelian hernia occurs higher on the anterior abdominal wall, along the semilunar line, not below the inguinal ligament.
An indirect inguinal hernia comes out above the inguinal ligament through the deep ring and the inguinal canal.
An obturator hernia is rarely palpable. It usually presents as bowel obstruction with medial thigh pain (Howship-Romberg sign) in thin elderly women.

headqa-2014-43.why: A cirrhotic with ascites and new hepatic encephalopathy needs a precipitant found, and SBP is a common one that is easy to miss. Diagnostic paracentesis (neutrophils over 250/mm3) is mandatory urgently in any cirrhotic admitted with ascites, especially with decompensation.
notes: Asterixis with confusion in known cirrhosis points to hepatic encephalopathy, not stroke; CT is kept for focal signs, head trauma or failure to improve.
Ascites is already obvious on examination, so ultrasound adds nothing urgent and does not identify the cause of the decompensation.
Hepatic encephalopathy is a clinical diagnosis; an EEG is not needed and would delay finding and treating the trigger.
HCC can cause decompensation, but imaging for it is not urgent; ruling out infection such as SBP comes first.

headqa-2014-47.why: Fever, jaundice and RUQ pain (Charcot triad) with choledocholithiasis, a dilated duct, tachycardia and borderline BP mean acute cholangitis. Antibiotics alone are not enough. Urgent biliary drainage is needed, and ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction is first line.
notes: Antibiotics and support with delayed cholecystectomy might suit simple biliary colic or mild cholecystitis, but obstructive cholangitis needs the bile duct drained.
Cholecystectomy removes the gallbladder but does not clear the obstructed common bile duct, which is causing the sepsis.
Percutaneous transhepatic drainage is the fallback when ERCP fails or is not possible; it is not first choice.
Emergency open surgery with duct exploration in a septic patient carries much higher morbidity and mortality than endoscopic drainage.

headqa-2014-48.why: Stroke risk in AF depends on risk factors, not on whether the AF is paroxysmal or persistent. Hypertension, diabetes and female sex give CHADS2 2 and CHA2DS2-VASc 3, so she needs long-term anticoagulation. Australian guidance uses CHA2DS2-VA (no sex point), which still scores 2, and prefers a DOAC.
notes: Paroxysmal AF carries roughly the same stroke risk as persistent AF, so being in sinus rhythm today does not remove the need to anticoagulate.
Age 75 or over and prior stroke are only some of the risk factors; her hypertension and diabetes alone are enough to justify anticoagulation.
Aspirin gives little stroke protection in AF and still causes bleeding, so it is not an acceptable substitute when risk scores call for anticoagulation.
Anticoagulating only during AF episodes does not work, because paroxysms are often silent; long-term oral anticoagulation is needed, not intermittent LMWH.

headqa-2014-49.why: In obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (LVOT gradient 70 mmHg), positive inotropes such as digoxin increase contractility and worsen the dynamic obstruction. Digoxin is contraindicated, while drugs that lower contractility or heart rate are the treatment of choice.
notes: Beta-blockers are first-line in symptomatic obstructive HCM: they lower contractility and heart rate and reduce the gradient.
Verapamil or diltiazem are the alternative when beta-blockers fail or are not tolerated, because they improve relaxation and reduce obstruction.
Unexplained exertional syncope and a family history of sudden death are major risk factors, so an ICD is indicated for primary prevention.
A resting gradient of 50 mmHg or more with symptoms is an indication for septal myectomy if drugs fail, so it is reasonable here.

headqa-2014-50.why: Ongoing ischaemic chest pain with LBBB, especially if new or of unknown duration, is treated as a STEMI equivalent because LBBB hides ST changes. Arrange reperfusion promptly and do not wait for troponin; Sgarbossa criteria help, but suspected ischaemia with LBBB still means primary PCI.
notes: Waiting for troponin delays reperfusion in a possible occlusion MI, and every minute of delay means more myocardium lost.
Isolated LBBB in sinus rhythm at 80 bpm is not an indication for pacing; reperfusion takes priority.
Oppressive chest pain with sweating in a diabetic smoker points to ACS, not PE, and CT pulmonary angiography would delay reperfusion.
Pericarditis gives pleuritic, positional pain with diffuse ST elevation, not LBBB; giving NSAIDs would miss an infarction.

headqa-2014-53.why: Resistant hypertension in an obese smoker with morning headache, daytime sleepiness and a non-dipping or reverse-dipping pattern on ABPM points to obstructive sleep apnoea. Overnight polysomnography is the test to confirm it. OSA is the most common secondary cause of resistant hypertension.
notes: Phaeochromocytoma causes episodes of headache, sweating and palpitations, not daytime sleepiness with nocturnal hypertension in an obese patient.
Primary aldosteronism should be screened for in resistant hypertension, but the morning headache, sleepiness and nocturnal pattern point first to sleep apnoea.
Doppler for renal artery stenosis would fit sudden worsening of hypertension or renal deterioration, neither of which is described here.
CT of the aorta looks for coarctation, which fits a young patient with arm-leg blood pressure difference or weak femoral pulses, not this picture.

headqa-2014-63.why: Pleural plaques are almost pathognomonic of asbestos exposure, and with them, basal-predominant reticular interstitial disease suggests asbestosis. The first step is a detailed occupational history, because the diagnosis rests on documented exposure plus compatible imaging, usually without biopsy.
notes: Smoking history is relevant to overall lung risk, but smoking does not cause pleural plaques, so it does not explain the defining finding.
Eosinophilia points to eosinophilic lung disease or parasites and has nothing to do with pleural plaques and basal fibrosis.
Lung function tests measure severity but do not identify the cause; finding out about exposure comes first.
Biopsy is invasive and usually not needed when exposure history and imaging are typical of asbestosis.

headqa-2014-70.why: Asymmetric onset of rigidity and bradykinesia, reduced arm swing and hypomimia, plus vivid dream-enacting nightmares (REM sleep behaviour disorder, a prodromal synucleinopathy feature), make idiopathic Parkinson's disease the most likely diagnosis.
notes: A lacunar infarct starts suddenly with hemiparesis or sensory loss; it does not cause slowly progressive rigidity, hypomimia and REM sleep behaviour disorder.
ALS causes weakness with mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs (fasciculations, hyperreflexia), not extrapyramidal rigidity and bradykinesia.
A cervical plexopathy would cause weakness, sensory loss and pain in a root or plexus distribution, not parkinsonism with hypomimia.
Corticobasal degeneration is asymmetric but has cortical signs such as apraxia, alien limb, cortical sensory loss and myoclonus; REM sleep behaviour disorder points to a synucleinopathy.

headqa-2014-78.why: The stem shows haemolysis: anaemia, high reticulocytes, raised LDH, unconjugated bilirubin, undetectable haptoglobin and splenomegaly. The next step is the direct Coombs (antiglobulin) test, which separates immune from non-immune haemolysis. Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia is the classic cause in an adult.
notes: Faecal occult blood investigates GI blood loss, which gives a low reticulocyte, iron-deficient microcytic picture, not high LDH and absent haptoglobin.
Haematinics fit hypoproliferative anaemia. The high reticulocyte count shows the marrow is responding, and the MCV of 100 fits reticulocytosis rather than B12/folate deficiency.
Ultrasound would only confirm splenomegaly, which is already palpable. It does not tell you the cause of the haemolysis.
Bone marrow aspirate is not needed when peripheral markers clearly show peripheral destruction with an appropriate reticulocyte response.

headqa-2014-79.why: Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (schistocytes, high LDH, absent haptoglobin, negative Coombs) with severe thrombocytopenia, neurological signs and normal coagulation is TTP. TTP is an emergency. Treat urgently with plasma exchange, usually with steroids; caplacizumab is now often added.
notes: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia gives a positive direct Coombs test and spherocytes, not schistocytes. It also does not explain platelets of 5,000.
Von Willebrand disease is a bleeding disorder. It does not cause haemolysis, schistocytes or neurological deficits, and desmopressin has no role here.
Immune thrombocytopenia does not cause schistocytic haemolysis. Platelet transfusion is relatively contraindicated in TTP because it may worsen thrombosis.
Evans syndrome is AIHA plus ITP, so the Coombs test would be positive and the smear would not show prominent schistocytes.

headqa-2014-80.why: Cataract surgery carries very low bleeding risk, so vitamin K antagonists should continue, keeping the INR in the therapeutic range. Interrupting anticoagulation with a mechanical mitral valve risks valve thrombosis. In Australia warfarin is the VKA used rather than acenocoumarol, but the principle is the same.
notes: Stopping the VKA with no bridging leaves a mechanical mitral valve unprotected for days, which is a high thrombotic risk, and it is unnecessary for a low-bleeding-risk procedure.
Interruption with LMWH bridging is meant for high-bleeding-risk surgery. It exposes the patient to needless thrombotic and bleeding risk for cataract surgery.
Fresh frozen plasma reversal is for urgent surgery or major bleeding. Neither applies to an elective, low-risk eye procedure.
Vitamin K reversal makes later re-anticoagulation difficult and puts the mechanical valve at risk. It is not indicated for cataract surgery.

headqa-2014-85.why: An unprovoked PE in a young woman with a prolonged aPTT that does not explain bleeding, mild thrombocytopenia, pregnancy loss and Raynaud's (possible SLE) strongly suggests antiphospholipid syndrome. Lupus anticoagulant explains the prolonged aPTT and is one of the defining laboratory tests.
notes: Antithrombin deficiency causes venous thrombosis but does not prolong the aPTT or cause thrombocytopenia, and there is no family history.
Factor V Leiden is the most common inherited thrombophilia, but it does not prolong the aPTT, lower platelets or fit Raynaud's.
Protein C deficiency does not explain the prolonged aPTT, the thrombocytopenia or the autoimmune features.
Protein S deficiency does not explain the prolonged aPTT and low platelets that together point to antiphospholipid antibodies.

headqa-2014-91.why: Polyuria with dilute urine after head trauma, no concentration during water deprivation, and a rise in urine osmolality of more than 50% (190 to 410) after desmopressin show ADH deficiency with intact renal response. This is central diabetes insipidus, now also called AVP deficiency.
notes: Primary polydipsia gives low-normal plasma osmolality and sodium and concentrates urine with water deprivation. Here plasma osmolality is high-normal and the urine does not concentrate.
Acute adrenal insufficiency presents with hypotension, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia, not high-volume dilute polyuria that corrects with desmopressin.
SIADH causes hyponatraemia with inappropriately concentrated urine and low urine output, which is the opposite of this picture.
Nephrogenic DI would show little or no rise in urine osmolality after desmopressin. The large response here shows the kidneys respond to ADH.

headqa-2014-95.why: Low basal cortisol that does not rise after ACTH stimulation, with markedly raised plasma ACTH, means the adrenal glands themselves have failed. That is primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's), here with weight loss, asthenia and anorexia.
notes: Secondary adrenal insufficiency has low or inappropriately normal ACTH. The ACTH here is four times the upper limit.
Hypothalamic (tertiary) insufficiency also gives low ACTH, so it cannot explain a markedly raised ACTH.
A corticotropinoma raises ACTH but drives cortisol excess (Cushing's disease), not low cortisol with a flat response to stimulation.
The results are conclusive: low cortisol, no response to ACTH and high ACTH together confirm primary adrenal failure.

headqa-2014-99.why: A middle-aged adult with nephrotic syndrome (proteinuria over 3.5 g/day, hypoalbuminaemia, hyperlipidaemia, oedema) and near-normal creatinine most likely has membranous nephropathy, the commonest primary cause in non-diabetic adults. Microscopic haematuria can occur. Check anti-PLA2R antibodies and look for secondary causes such as malignancy.
notes: Minimal change disease is the main cause in children and is rare in a 47-year-old, and haematuria is uncommon.
FSGS is a common cause of adult nephrotic syndrome, especially in Black patients and with obesity or HIV, but it is less likely than membranous at this age.
MPGN type I usually gives a mixed nephritic-nephrotic picture with low complement and is often linked to hepatitis C; this stem is mainly nephrotic.
Mesangial proliferative GN, such as IgA nephropathy, usually shows haematuria with less proteinuria and rarely causes full nephrotic syndrome.

headqa-2015-104.why: In an injecting drug user, severe limb pain out of proportion to minimal skin signs with septic shock, confusion and kidney injury suggests necrotising fasciitis with streptococcal toxic shock. It needs urgent surgical debridement and antibiotics, including clindamycin.
notes: Clostridial gas gangrene usually follows trauma or deep wounds and gives crepitus and marked myonecrosis with very high CK. The CK here is normal.
Mycobacterial skin infection is indolent and develops over weeks. It does not cause hyperacute septic shock within 24 hours.
Erysipelas causes a sharply demarcated, raised, red plaque. The absence of obvious skin changes despite severe pain and shock argues against it.

headqa-2015-105.why: In suspected bacterial meningitis with shock and coma, give antibiotics without delay. Take blood cultures, resuscitate with fluids, and give dexamethasone with empirical ceftriaxone plus vancomycin, adding ampicillin for Listeria because he is over 50; CT and LP come after. Australian eTG uses benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin for Listeria cover.
notes: Waiting for CT, fundoscopy and CSF results before giving antibiotics delays treatment that saves lives and increases mortality in a septic, comatose patient.
Holding back antibiotics until he is haemodynamically stable is dangerous, and fluids should come before vasopressors in initial resuscitation.
This regimen gives no Listeria cover and no dexamethasone, skips blood cultures and fluids, and ceftazidime is not first-line for community-acquired meningitis.

headqa-2015-106.why: A lymphocytic exudate (90% lymphocytes, high protein and LDH) that is not malignant, in a young man from a high-TB country who did not respond to antibiotics, points to tuberculous pleuritis. A high pleural fluid ADA has high sensitivity and specificity for this.
notes: CT shows the anatomy, such as loculation and the pleura, but cannot confirm tuberculosis as the cause.
Pleural pH helps decide whether a parapneumonic effusion needs drainage, but it does not identify tuberculosis in a lymphocytic exudate.
A tuberculin test only shows infection, not disease, and is often negative in TB pleuritis. A positive result is also common in people from endemic areas.

headqa-2015-119.why: Night-time cough and wheeze in an atopic patient suggest asthma, but spirometry and the bronchodilator test are normal. The next step is a bronchial challenge such as methacholine to show airway hyperresponsiveness, which has a high negative predictive value.
notes: Sinus X-ray is of little value and would not confirm or exclude asthma as the cause of the wheeze.
With a normal chest X-ray and a typical asthma picture, CT adds radiation without answering the question.
A skin prick test shows allergic sensitisation, which is already likely given her atopic rhinitis, but it does not confirm asthma.

headqa-2015-138.why: This is SLE with mild-to-moderate disease: arthritis, serositis and malar rash, with no kidney or CNS involvement. First-line treatment is NSAIDs plus an antimalarial (hydroxychloroquine, the standard in Australia), with low-dose steroids only if needed.
notes: High-dose glucocorticoids are kept for severe organ-threatening lupus such as nephritis or CNS disease, which this patient does not have.
Mycophenolate is induction therapy for lupus nephritis or severe disease and is not needed for joints, skin and pleura alone.
Active SLE with high-titre anti-dsDNA needs treatment, and hydroxychloroquine is advised for almost every patient to reduce flares and damage.

headqa-2015-139.why: An older woman with polymyalgia symptoms, jaw claudication and sudden painless monocular loss with an afferent pupillary defect has giant cell arteritis until proven otherwise. ESR/CRP is the quick first test. In Australia, start high-dose steroids straight away and confirm with temporal artery ultrasound or biopsy.
notes: Lumbar puncture has no role here: there are no meningeal signs, no fever and nothing to suggest raised intracranial pressure, and it would not show arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy.
MR angiography may show large-vessel involvement but is not the first test; a cheap, fast inflammatory marker supports the diagnosis while urgent steroids are started.
Carotid ultrasound looks for embolic amaurosis or retinal artery occlusion, but polymyalgia, weight loss and jaw claudication in a 70-year-old point to giant cell arteritis, not atheroma.

headqa-2015-144.why: A rising ANCA titre alone, with no clinical, radiological, blood or urine signs of activity, does not justify immunosuppression. It predicts relapse poorly, so the right approach is closer monitoring.
notes: Steroids for an isolated serological change in an asymptomatic patient expose him to toxicity without proven benefit.
Cyclophosphamide is induction therapy for active severe GPA and is not justified without disease activity.
Mycophenolate is not indicated for an isolated ANCA rise with no clinical relapse.

headqa-2015-161.why: Dyspareunia, cyclical dyschezia and rectal bleeding, dysmenorrhoea, infertility and a tender posterior fornix suggest deep endometriosis. Laparoscopy with biopsy and histology gives the definitive diagnosis. Current Australian and ESHRE guidance also accepts expert ultrasound or MRI to make the diagnosis without surgery.
notes: Transvaginal ultrasound is a good first-line test for endometriomas and deep nodules, but it depends on the operator and misses superficial peritoneal disease, so it cannot give a certain diagnosis.
MRI helps map deep rectovaginal or bowel disease before surgery, but it is not the test that confirms the diagnosis by histology.
Colonoscopy usually looks normal because the endometriosis invades the bowel from the outside (serosa) inward, so it rarely shows lesions and cannot confirm the diagnosis.

headqa-2015-170.why: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is low-to-intermediate risk, and he has excellent functional capacity (more than 4 METs) with no cardiac symptoms. No stress testing or imaging is needed, but a baseline ECG is reasonable given his age and hypertension.
notes: Stress testing does not change management when functional capacity is above 4 METs and there are no symptoms.
Echocardiography is only indicated for murmurs, dyspnoea or suspected heart failure, and none is present here.
Pharmacological perfusion imaging is for patients with poor or unknown functional capacity before higher-risk surgery.

headqa-2015-175.why: SSRIs such as paroxetine are among the strongest drug risk factors for falls in older people, through sedation, slowed reactions, impaired balance and hyponatraemia. Paroxetine is also anticholinergic. The stem points away from the antihypertensives by stating there are no postural blood pressure changes and no dizziness.
notes: Allopurinol does not affect balance, alertness or blood pressure, so it is not a recognised fall-risk drug.
Thiazides can cause falls through orthostatic hypotension or hyponatraemia, but the stem specifically says there is no postural drop and no dizziness.
ACE inhibitors cause falls mainly through hypotension, which the stem excludes by documenting no postural change and no presyncope.

headqa-2015-176.why: This is a grade 2 follicular lymphoma with low tumour burden: she has no symptoms, normal blood counts and LDH, nodes under 3 cm, no splenomegaly and a low beta2-microglobulin, so she meets no GELF criteria. Asymptomatic low-burden indolent lymphoma is watched without treatment, because treating early does not improve survival.
notes: R-CHOP is used for follicular lymphoma that needs treatment or has transformed, and it brings anthracycline toxicity in a woman with heart failure. She has no indication for treatment.
R-CVP is a choice once follicular lymphoma meets criteria for treatment, but her disease is asymptomatic and low burden, so it is not indicated yet.
Rituximab-bendamustine is a standard first-line regimen once treatment criteria are met, but her low-burden asymptomatic disease does not yet need treatment.

headqa-2015-177.why: He has a single 3 cm liver metastasis with no other disease on CT and PET. Isolated metachronous colorectal liver metastases should be assessed for resection first, because surgery offers a chance of long-term cure.
notes: FOLFIRI plus bevacizumab is used for unresectable metastatic disease, or as conversion therapy. It is not first-line for a single resectable liver lesion.
Single-agent capecitabine is a palliative or low-intensity option and would give up the chance of cure in a fit patient with one resectable metastasis.
Liver radiotherapy, such as SBRT, is reserved for patients who cannot have surgery. Resection remains the standard of care for a single resectable metastasis.

headqa-2015-188.why: A patient who wants to go home despite clear safety concerns, such as being unable to give his own insulin, poor control and self-neglect, needs a formal assessment of decision-making capacity first. This determines whether his refusal of help must be respected or whether substitute decision-making applies.
notes: Involving primary care and social work matters for discharge planning, but he has already refused help, so you first need to know whether he has capacity to refuse it.
Dementia screening may be useful, but a diagnosis of dementia does not settle whether he can make this specific decision; capacity is assessed decision by decision.
Depression could affect his judgement and should be considered, but it is part of the wider picture, not the step that decides whether his choice to go home is valid.

headqa-2015-192.why: Both exposure (per-capita meat consumption) and outcome (colon cancer incidence) were measured at the level of whole countries, not individuals. A study whose unit of analysis is a population group is ecological, and its conclusions are open to the ecological fallacy.
notes: A case series describes individual patients who share a condition and has no comparison of exposure across populations.
A case-cohort study samples individuals from a defined cohort and compares cases with a subcohort. Here no individual-level data were collected.
A cross-sectional study measures exposure and outcome in individuals at one point in time. This study used aggregate country-level data.

headqa-2015-193.why: A random sample of patients was assessed once, recording current lipid-lowering drug use and diabetes status at the same time, with no follow-up and no selection by outcome. That is a cross-sectional (prevalence) study, which shows association but not which came first.
notes: A case-control study selects participants by outcome (diabetes or no diabetes) and then looks back at exposure. Here the sample was random and not chosen by outcome.
A prospective cohort study follows people grouped by exposure over time to see who develops the outcome. Here both were recorded at a single point.
A randomised trial assigns the intervention. In this study drug use was only observed.

headqa-2015-213.why: Asymmetric oligoarthritis, conjunctivitis, circinate balanitis and psoriasiform palmoplantar lesions (keratoderma blennorrhagicum) after a sexual exposure 20 days earlier make up the classic picture of Reiter syndrome. This is now called reactive arthritis, usually triggered by Chlamydia.
notes: Acute HIV causes a mononucleosis-like illness with a maculopapular rash, but not this combination of conjunctivitis, balanitis, asymmetric arthritis and keratoderma.
Secondary syphilis also affects the palms and soles, but it usually appears 4 to 10 weeks after exposure and does not explain conjunctivitis with asymmetric oligoarthritis.
Erythema multiforme causes target lesions and mucosal erosions, often after HSV or drugs, but not psoriasiform palmoplantar plaques or inflammatory arthritis.

headqa-2015-217.why: An elderly woman has subacute vision loss with metamorphopsia, and the macula shows exudates, deep haemorrhages and neurosensory detachment, all signs of choroidal neovascularisation. Soft drusen in the other eye confirm the underlying AMD. Neovascular (wet) AMD is treated with intravitreal anti-VEGF injections.
notes: Posterior vitreous detachment causes floaters and flashes, not metamorphopsia, macular exudates, haemorrhages or subretinal fluid.
Central retinal artery occlusion causes sudden painless profound vision loss with a pale retina and a cherry-red spot, not exudates and neurosensory detachment.
NAION causes sudden vision loss with a swollen optic disc and altitudinal field loss. The macula is not affected and metamorphopsia does not occur.

headqa-2015-226.why: Carcinoma in situ (Tis) confined to the head of a pedunculated polyp that has been completely removed carries almost no risk of lymph node spread. Polypectomy is therefore curative and only colonoscopic surveillance is needed.
notes: Segmental colectomy is for invasive cancer with high-risk features such as stalk or margin involvement, lymphovascular invasion or poor differentiation, none of which apply here.
Further local excision of the base is only needed if margins are involved or excision was incomplete, but here the in situ disease is confined to the head.
Oncological resection with lymphadenectomy is for invasive carcinoma with risk of nodal spread, but in situ disease cannot metastasise.

headqa-2015-32.why: Chronic watery diarrhoea with normal-looking mucosa points to microscopic colitis. A thickened subepithelial band that stains with Masson trichrome (collagen, over 10 µm), with surface epithelial damage and more intraepithelial lymphocytes, defines collagenous colitis.
notes: Ulcerative colitis would show continuous friable or ulcerated mucosa on endoscopy, with crypt distortion and crypt abscesses, not a subepithelial collagen band.
Pseudomembranous colitis shows yellow-white plaques on endoscopy and 'volcano' exudates of fibrin and neutrophils on histology, usually after antibiotics.
Fibrosing Crohn's causes transmural fibrosis with strictures and often ulcers or granulomas, not a thin subepithelial collagen layer under normal-looking mucosa.

headqa-2015-50.why: A lesion that starts on a digit after gardening and then spreads as nodules up the arm along the lymphatics, with no fever, is sporotrichoid lymphocutaneous spread. Sporothrix schenckii from soil or plants is the classic cause, and it is confirmed by culture of a biopsy.
notes: Microsporum gypseum (a soil dermatophyte) causes a superficial annular, scaly tinea, not nodules spreading along lymphatics over weeks.
Staphylococcus aureus lymphangitis comes on acutely over hours to days, usually with fever and pus, not as a slow 3-week chain of nodules.
Mycobacterium marinum also spreads in a sporotrichoid pattern, but it follows fish tank or water exposure, not gardening.

headqa-2015-56.why: In infective endocarditis, severe aortic regurgitation (EROA 0.5 cm2) with heart failure that does not respond to treatment is an indication for emergency surgery. New complete heart block suggests a perivalvular abscess, which also needs surgery. Replace the valve and continue targeted antibiotics. S. gallolyticus also calls for a colonoscopy.
notes: A balloon pump is contraindicated in significant aortic regurgitation, and delaying surgery for 3 weeks in refractory heart failure from endocarditis is unsafe.
Percutaneous aortic valve implantation is not appropriate in active endocarditis because the infected tissue and any abscess cannot be removed.
A permanent pacemaker during active bacteraemia risks infecting the device, and it does nothing for the valve lesion that is causing the refractory heart failure.

headqa-2015-57.why: This is an anterior STEMI with cardiogenic shock (BP 68/32) and pulmonary oedema. Urgent primary PCI to restore blood flow is the treatment that improves survival in shock, and it is preferred over fibrinolysis.
notes: Nitrates are contraindicated with a systolic pressure this low because they worsen the hypotension.
Fibrinolysis works less well in cardiogenic shock and is only a fallback if timely PCI is not available.
Furosemide does not treat the cause, and it can worsen hypotension in shock; it is not the key decision here.

headqa-2015-71.why: A young atopic patient (asthma, multiple allergies) with repeated, self-resolving food bolus impactions fits eosinophilic esophagitis. It is the leading cause of food impaction in young adults, and the diagnosis needs biopsies showing at least 15 eosinophils per high-power field.
notes: Barrett's esophagus causes no symptoms of its own. It follows long-standing reflux in older patients and does not cause episodes of bolus impaction.
A Schatzki ring causes intermittent 'steakhouse' impaction, but usually in people over 40, and it has no link to atopy.
Infectious esophagitis causes painful swallowing in immunocompromised patients, not recurrent food impaction in an atopic young person.

headqa-2015-74.why: Ascitic neutrophils are 60% of 2,300 cells/mL, about 1,380/mL, which is well above the threshold of 250/mL. That makes this spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, even without fever. Start an IV third-generation cephalosporin (cefotaxime, or ceftriaxone as usually used in Australia) straight away, with albumin when indicated.
notes: Salt restriction is part of long-term ascites management, but it does not treat the infection, which is the urgent problem.
Spironolactone treats ascites over the long term but does nothing for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, which needs immediate antibiotics.
Large-volume paracentesis is for tense or refractory ascites and is not the priority when the fluid shows infection.

headqa-2015-81.why: Thyrotoxicosis with suppressed TSH, no uptake on the scan and no goitre points to exogenous thyroxine. Low thyroglobulin is the decisive finding, because taking thyroxine suppresses the gland's own thyroglobulin output.
notes: Graves' disease shows diffuse high uptake on the scan and usually a goitre, with normal or raised thyroglobulin.
Struma ovarii shows little uptake in the neck but uptake in the pelvis, and thyroglobulin is raised because the ovarian tissue makes hormone.
Subacute thyroiditis has low uptake but a tender gland and a high ESR, and thyroglobulin is raised as follicles break down.

headqa-2015-83.why: The episodes are hypoglycaemia (adrenergic and neuroglycopenic symptoms relieved by eating), and HbA1c 5.9% means he is over-treated. Sulfonylureas such as glimepiride release insulin whatever the glucose level and cause hypoglycaemia. Metformin does not, so the sulfonylurea is the drug to stop.
notes: Diet changes will not fix hypoglycaemia caused by a high-dose sulfonylurea when HbA1c is already 5.9%. The cause is the drug, not how carbohydrate is spread through the day.
Metformin on its own almost never causes hypoglycaemia and is the first-line drug to keep. Stopping it would remove the safest agent and leave the one causing the problem.
DPP-4 inhibitors and metformin carry little risk of hypoglycaemia, so this swap does nothing about the cause. Glimepiride would still be driving the episodes.

headqa-2015-86.why: Prolactin of 480 µg/L with a 35 mm adenoma is a macroprolactinoma. Dopamine agonists are first-line even when there is chiasmal compression and a visual field defect, because they usually shrink the tumour and restore vision quickly. Cabergoline is the preferred agent in Australia.
notes: Surgery is kept for resistance to or intolerance of dopamine agonists, apoplexy, or a non-prolactin-secreting tumour. Visual loss from a prolactinoma does not by itself call for surgery first.
Radiotherapy is a third-line option for tumours that resist both medical and surgical treatment. It acts slowly and causes hypopituitarism.
His hypogonadotropic hypogonadism comes from high prolactin suppressing GnRH. It often recovers once prolactin falls, so testosterone is not the first step.

headqa-2015-93.why: Skin necrosis that starts soon after a vitamin K antagonist is begun points to protein C deficiency. Protein C has a short half-life and falls before factors II and X, so a transient prothrombotic state causes microvascular thrombosis. In Australia warfarin, not acenocoumarol, is the usual vitamin K antagonist.
notes: Antithrombin deficiency causes venous thrombosis and heparin resistance, not necrosis triggered by starting a vitamin K antagonist, because antithrombin levels do not depend on vitamin K.
Factor V Leiden is the commonest inherited cause of venous thromboembolism, but it is not linked to necrosis after starting a coumarin, because it does not create the early protein C drop.
Hyperhomocysteinaemia raises arterial and venous thrombotic risk, but it has nothing to do with vitamin K and does not explain necrosis timed to coumarin initiation.

headqa-2016-107.why: Babesia is a tick-borne protozoan that infects red cells. It causes fever and haemolysis, and on Giemsa smear its ring forms (sometimes tetrads, the Maltese cross) look like Plasmodium falciparum. It is the tick-borne infection most easily mistaken for malaria.
notes: Borrelia burgdorferi causes Lyme disease, with erythema migrans, arthritis and neurological features. It does not cause haemolysis or intra-erythrocytic forms.
Francisella tularensis causes ulceroglandular or pneumonic tularaemia. It is not a red-cell parasite and does not look like malaria on a smear.
Rickettsia conorii causes Mediterranean spotted fever, with fever, rash and an eschar (tache noire). It lives in endothelial cells, not red cells.

headqa-2016-117.why: Severe acute pyelonephritis needs effective treatment, so a placebo control is unethical and the new drug must be compared with a standard antibiotic. Randomisation and double blinding cut bias. A parallel design suits an acute illness that is cured, because crossover is impossible.
notes: Giving placebo for severe pyelonephritis would be unethical. Open-label, unrandomised allocation would also introduce bias.
Crossover designs need a stable, chronic condition that returns to baseline between periods. An acute infection that is cured cannot be crossed over, and open-label adds bias.
This combines two problems: placebo in a serious infection is unethical, and a crossover design does not suit an acute illness that is cured.

headqa-2016-131.why: Exposure (vitamin D level) and outcome (metabolic syndrome) are both measured once, at the same visit, in a sample of the population. That is a cross-sectional design. It estimates prevalence and association but cannot show which came first.
notes: A prospective cohort would follow people grouped by vitamin D status over time to see who develops metabolic syndrome, but here there is a single visit with no follow-up.
A case-control study would choose people by outcome (with and without metabolic syndrome) and then look back at exposure, whereas here unselected adults are sampled and both are measured together.
A case-crossover study compares a transient exposure just before an acute event with earlier control periods in the same person, so it does not fit a chronic condition measured once.

headqa-2016-133.why: For a very rare outcome with a long latency, a case-control study is the design of choice. It starts from the people who already have the reaction and compares their past drug exposure with controls, which is efficient when there are few events.
notes: Clinical trials are too small and too short to detect a very rare, delayed adverse reaction, and deliberately exposing people to a suspected harm is unethical.
A prevalence study measures exposure and outcome at one point in time. It would capture too few cases of a rare event and cannot show which came first.
An ecological study uses group-level data, so it cannot link drug exposure to the reaction in individuals and is prone to the ecological fallacy.

headqa-2016-134.why: The risk attributable to exposure among the exposed is the risk difference: incidence in the exposed minus incidence in the unexposed. Here that is 15 − 5 = 10 per 1000 per year.
notes: 20 per 1000 comes from adding the two incidences together, which has no epidemiological meaning.
15 per 1000 is the total incidence in hypertensive people. It includes the baseline risk that is not due to hypertension.
3 is the relative risk (15/5). It is a ratio with no units, not an excess incidence per 1000 per year.

headqa-2016-140.why: His tests were normal a month ago. Since the knee injury he has likely been taking more naproxen, and now he has kidney failure, hematuria without proteinuria, sloughed papillary cells and papillary necrosis on ultrasound. NSAIDs cause papillary necrosis, and risk is higher with diabetes, an ACE inhibitor plus a diuretic, and older age.
notes: He had been on enalapril long term with normal kidney function, and an ACE inhibitor alone would not cause papillary necrosis or shed papillary cells.
Diabetic nephropathy progresses over years with proteinuria, but here proteinuria is negative and kidney function was normal a month ago.
A CPK of 45 U/L is normal, which rules out rhabdomyolysis, and rhabdomyolysis would not cause papillary necrosis.

headqa-2016-156.why: A teenager with morning jerks in both arms while fully conscious, daily absences and a tonic-clonic seizure after sleep loss and alcohol, plus a family history, has juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. This is a genetic generalised epilepsy, and these triggers are typical of it.
notes: Lennox-Gastaut starts in early childhood with tonic seizures, intellectual disability and slow spike-wave on EEG, none of which fits a 15-year-old with this history.
Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy causes focal seizures with automatisms but not morning myoclonic jerks in both arms, and it is not usually triggered by sleep loss in a family pattern.
Alcohol here is only a trigger: months of morning myoclonus and daily absences plus a family history point to an underlying epilepsy, not a drug effect.

headqa-2016-162.why: A 4 cm intramural fibroid in a woman with completed family, only mildly heavy periods and no other symptoms needs no treatment. Monitor it with a repeat ultrasound. Treatment is for fibroids causing significant symptoms, anaemia, infertility or rapid growth.
notes: Myomectomy is for symptomatic fibroids or fibroids affecting fertility, and this woman is basically asymptomatic and has completed her family.
