Hysterectomy is major surgery and far too much for a small fibroid that is causing almost no symptoms.
GnRH analogues work only temporarily, cause menopausal side effects and are mainly used before surgery, so they have no role in an asymptomatic fibroid.

headqa-2016-163.why: The ultrasound shows a 25 mm well-defined lesion inside the uterine cavity, most likely a submucosal fibroid or polyp, causing heavy periods. Hysteroscopy lets you see the lesion, biopsy it and remove it in the same procedure, so it is the standard approach for a focal lesion in the cavity.
notes: A blind endometrial aspirate can miss a focal lesion and does not treat it, and endometrial cancer risk is low at 31.
The combined pill may reduce bleeding but leaves a structural lesion undiagnosed and untreated.
Tranexamic acid only controls symptoms and does nothing to diagnose or remove the lesion causing the bleeding.

headqa-2016-168.why: Painless bright red bleeding at 32 weeks in a woman with a previous caesarean, with mother and fetus both stable, suggests placenta praevia. Locate the placenta by ultrasound first. Transvaginal ultrasound is safe and more accurate than transabdominal, whereas a digital exam is avoided.
notes: An emergency caesarean is only needed for heavy bleeding, maternal instability or fetal distress, and here mother and fetus are both stable.
Induction of labour is contraindicated if placenta praevia has not been excluded, and the baby is preterm at 32 weeks.
Artificial rupture of membranes is contraindicated with possible placenta praevia and is not appropriate in a stable preterm pregnancy.

headqa-2016-171.why: The excision showed a 6 mm invasive ductal carcinoma, so the axilla now has to be staged. In a clinically node-negative axilla this is done by sentinel lymph node biopsy. Margins are clear, and adjuvant radiotherapy and endocrine therapy are planned once nodal status is known.
notes: Radiotherapy plus endocrine therapy will probably be needed after breast-conserving surgery, but the invasive disease has not been staged, so the axilla must be assessed first.
Mastectomy is not needed for a small, completely excised tumour, and axillary dissection is not done in a clinically node-negative axilla before a sentinel node result.
Chemotherapy is not indicated before staging, and this small luminal A–like tumour (strongly ER/PR positive, Ki-67 10%, HER2 negative) is unlikely to need it.

headqa-2016-174.why: Cyanosis in the legs but pink face and hands is differential cyanosis. It occurs when a patent ductus reverses (Eisenmenger) and sends deoxygenated blood into the aorta beyond the arm and head arteries. The long-standing murmur fits an untreated PDA.
notes: Tetralogy of Fallot causes cyanosis of the whole body, not just the lower limbs.
Eisenmenger from a VSD mixes blood inside the heart, so cyanosis affects the whole body equally.
Coarctation causes a blood pressure and pulse difference between arms and legs, not lower-limb cyanosis in a 9-year-old.

headqa-2016-181.why: A young infant with bilateral grade III reflux who has had pyelonephritis is at risk of repeat infection and kidney scarring. Give continuous antibiotic prophylaxis and do a DMSA scan to look for scarring. Australian practice usually uses trimethoprim or cefalexin for prophylaxis.
notes: Reflux may resolve over time, but after pyelonephritis with bilateral grade III reflux, doing nothing risks repeat infection and scarring.
Endoscopic correction is not first line at 2 months and is kept for breakthrough infections despite prophylaxis or persistent high-grade reflux.
Routine monthly urine cultures without prophylaxis do not prevent repeat pyelonephritis and are not recommended in a child without symptoms.

headqa-2016-191.why: Synovial fluid with 20,000 white cells/mm3, 85% neutrophils and no crystals, in a diabetic patient recently in hospital who now has leucocytosis, should be treated as septic arthritis. A negative Gram stain does not exclude infection. Admit, give IV antibiotics until the culture result is back, and drain the joint. In Australia, eTG suggests IV flucloxacillin, adding vancomycin if MRSA is a risk.
notes: Injecting a steroid into a joint that may be infected is contraindicated and could make a septic arthritis much worse.
Possible septic arthritis needs admission and IV antibiotics; treating as an outpatient with oral antibiotics and waiting a week risks destroying the joint.
No crystals were seen, so there is no evidence of gout, and steroids with allopurinol would leave a probable infection untreated.

headqa-2016-192.why: Recurrent oral ulcers plus genital ulcers with erythema nodosum-like lesions point to Behçet syndrome. Recurrent oral aphthae are the essential criterion, and genital ulcers, skin lesions, eye and pathergy findings support it.
notes: Sarcoidosis causes erythema nodosum but not recurrent oral and genital ulceration.
Dermatomyositis presents with proximal weakness, heliotrope rash and Gottron papules, not mucosal ulcers or nodules.
SLE can cause oral ulcers, but recurrent genital ulcers with erythema nodosum are typical of Behçet, and lupus is far more common in women.

headqa-2016-193.why: A young man with inflammatory nocturnal low back and buttock pain, dactylitis ('sausage toes'), seronegativity and raised CRP has spondyloarthritis. Ask about psoriasis (psoriatic arthritis) and check HLA-B27.
notes: Gout does not cause inflammatory nocturnal back and buttock pain, and allopurinol is not started without a confirmed diagnosis or during acute inflammation.
Disc herniation gives mechanical pain that eases with rest, not nocturnal inflammatory pain with dactylitis and high CRP; surgical referral is not indicated.
Methotrexate does not work for axial disease; NSAIDs come first, then biologics for axial spondyloarthritis, and the diagnosis must be confirmed first.

headqa-2016-203.why: Loss of active knee extension with a low-lying patella (patella baja) means quadriceps tendon rupture, because the patella is no longer pulled up. Gout and chronic steroids are classic risk factors in older patients.
notes: Osteonecrosis causes knee pain but leaves the extensor mechanism intact, so it does not cause patella baja or loss of extension.
Gouty arthritis gives a hot, swollen, painful joint but does not change patellar height or abolish active extension.
Patellar tendon rupture also abolishes extension, but the patella rides high (patella alta); it is more typical in younger patients.

headqa-2016-213.why: Proximal weakness that improves with sustained exercise, increments on repetitive nerve stimulation, and a smoker's lung mass (likely small cell carcinoma) mean Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, caused by antibodies to presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels.
notes: Paraneoplastic neuropathy (e.g. anti-Hu sensory neuronopathy) causes sensory loss and does not produce an incremental response or improve with exercise.
Polymyositis causes fixed proximal weakness with raised CK; it does not fluctuate, cause diplopia or give an increment on repetitive stimulation.
Alcoholic myopathy does not fluctuate, improve with effort or show increments on repetitive stimulation.

headqa-2016-225.why: GCS 4 (8 or below), hypoventilation, hypoxaemia and signs of herniation (blown pupil, Cushing triad) mean the airway comes first. Secure it with endotracheal intubation while protecting the cervical spine, as in any major trauma.
notes: A laryngeal mask is a rescue airway; it does not give a definitive protected airway or allow controlled ventilation in severe TBI.
Mannitol may follow for herniation, but airway and breathing come first, and hypoxia and hypercapnia make intracranial hypertension worse.
A Venturi mask does not protect the airway or fix hypoventilation in a comatose patient breathing 8 times a minute.

headqa-2016-230.why: Renal colic with microscopic haematuria is best confirmed by non-contrast helical CT, the most sensitive and specific test for stones of any composition, including radiolucent uric acid stones.
notes: A plain abdominal X-ray misses radiolucent stones (e.g. uric acid) and small or overlying stones, so its sensitivity is low.
Ultrasound avoids radiation and shows hydronephrosis, but it is poor for ureteric stones, so it is less sensitive than CT.
Intravenous urography is outdated, needs contrast, and has been replaced by non-contrast CT because it is less sensitive.

headqa-2016-232.why: Macroscopic haematuria at the same time as a mucosal infection (pharyngitis, gastroenteritis, otitis), recurring and self-limited, is typical of IgA nephropathy (synpharyngitic haematuria). Post-streptococcal GN has a 1 to 3 week latency and does not recur.
notes: Membranoproliferative GN usually presents with nephritic or nephrotic syndrome and persistently low complement, not recurrent self-limited haematuria with each infection.
X-linked Alport syndrome typically affects boys with persistent haematuria, sensorineural deafness and eye changes; the episodes are not tied to infection.
Post-infectious GN follows infection after a latent period of 1 to 3 weeks and does not usually recur; haematuria starting during the infection argues against it.

headqa-2016-34.why: Patchy, heterogeneous involvement with fibrotic areas alternating with preserved lung, prominent fibroblastic foci and a subpleural, basal predominance is the textbook histological pattern of usual interstitial pneumonia. Temporal and spatial heterogeneity with fibroblastic foci is the key point to remember.
notes: Langerhans cell histiocytosis affects young smokers, favours the upper lobes, and shows peribronchiolar stellate nodules with Langerhans cells, not basal subpleural fibrosis with fibroblastic foci.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (extrinsic allergic alveolitis) shows bronchiolocentric lymphocytic inflammation with poorly formed granulomas, often worst in the upper and mid zones, and needs an antigen exposure, which this stem does not mention.
Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis fills the alveoli with PAS-positive lipoproteinaceous material while the architecture stays preserved; it does not cause septal fibrosis or fibroblastic foci.

headqa-2016-37.why: Thiopurine methyltransferase inactivates azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine. Homozygous-deficient patients build up toxic thioguanine nucleotides and develop severe myelosuppression. TPMT activity or genotype is checked before starting a thiopurine.
notes: Warfarin sensitivity is linked to CYP2C9 and VKORC1 polymorphisms, not TPMT, and the main risk is bleeding rather than marrow toxicity.
Isoniazid toxicity is linked to slow N-acetyltransferase 2 (NAT2) acetylator status and causes neuropathy and hepatotoxicity, not TPMT-related cytopenias.
Prolonged apnoea after succinylcholine comes from pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase) deficiency, not TPMT.

headqa-2016-44.why: In systole the contracting left ventricular wall compresses the intramyocardial vessels, so left coronary flow is mostly diastolic. Flow peaks in early diastole, when the myocardium relaxes and aortic pressure is still high.
notes: In isovolumetric contraction, wall tension rises sharply and squeezes the intramural vessels, so left coronary flow falls to its lowest point and may even reverse briefly.
Aortic pressure peaks in mid-systole, when myocardial compression is limiting flow, so the high driving pressure does not produce maximal left coronary flow.
Aortic flow peaks during early ejection, while the ventricle is contracting and restricting its own coronary perfusion.

headqa-2016-53.why: Carbapenems are the treatment of choice for serious infections such as bacteraemia caused by ESBL-producing Enterobacterales, which the MERINO trial supported. Ertapenem is suitable for a stable patient, and in Australia meropenem is often preferred if the patient is critically ill.
notes: ESBL enzymes are poorly reliably inhibited by clavulanate in serious infections, and amoxicillin-clavulanate is not adequate for ESBL bacteraemia.
Piperacillin-tazobactam was inferior to meropenem for ESBL E. coli bloodstream infection in the MERINO trial, so it is not the best choice for sepsis.
ESBL strains often carry fluoroquinolone resistance too, so ciprofloxacin is unreliable as empirical treatment for sepsis before susceptibility results are known.

headqa-2016-62.why: BP stays high despite full doses of three drugs, one of them a diuretic, and good adherence. The first step is ambulatory BP monitoring to rule out pseudo-resistance (white-coat effect) before confirming true resistant hypertension. Australian guidance agrees.
notes: Adding a fourth drug such as spironolactone is right for true resistant hypertension, but this must be confirmed with out-of-office readings first.
All three drugs are already at full dose (amlodipine 10 mg, losartan 100 mg, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg), so increasing a dose is not possible or useful.
Testing for secondary causes is done once resistant hypertension is confirmed, and ABPM comes first to exclude white-coat hypertension.

headqa-2016-74.why: Cancer arising in long-standing ulcerative colitis, with colitis still active, means the whole colonic mucosa is at risk of further cancers. Restorative proctocolectomy with an ileal pouch and a defunctioning ileostomy treats the cancer and the disease together. Low-risk T2N0 disease does not need neoadjuvant therapy.
notes: Anterior resection would leave diseased, actively inflamed colon at high risk of synchronous or metachronous cancer, so it suits only sporadic rectal cancer.
A tumour 8 cm from the anal verge allows sphincter preservation, and abdominoperineal resection still leaves the colitic colon in place.
Organ-preserving radiotherapy with local excision is not appropriate in UC, where the remaining mucosa keeps its cancer risk, and pelvic radiation harms a later pouch.

headqa-2016-86.why: This is a large multinodular goitre with a retrosternal part, compressive dysphagia, subclinical hyperthyroidism (suppressed TSH, normal free T4) and a growing nodule. Total thyroidectomy relieves compression, cures the hyperthyroidism and removes the risk of a false-negative biopsy. Compressive or intrathoracic goitre is a surgical problem.
notes: Watching is not enough once there are compressive symptoms, intrathoracic extension, a growing nodule and suppressed TSH in a patient with atrial fibrillation.
Radioiodine shrinks a large multinodular goitre only partly and slowly, and can cause swelling in an already compressive retrosternal goitre, so it is for patients unfit for surgery.
Antithyroid drugs would control the subclinical hyperthyroidism but do nothing for the size of the goitre or the dysphagia, and toxic nodular goitre relapses when they stop.

headqa-2016-91.why: A young patient with a gastrin-secreting pancreatic islet tumour (gastrinoma) and hypercalcaemia from primary hyperparathyroidism fits MEN1 (the three Ps: parathyroid, pancreas, pituitary). The MEN1 gene encodes menin.
notes: McCune-Albright syndrome combines polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, café-au-lait macules and precocious puberty from a GNAS mutation, not gastrinoma with hyperparathyroidism.
Carney complex involves cardiac myxomas, spotty skin pigmentation and primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease, not pancreatic gastrinoma.
Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1 causes hypoparathyroidism (hypocalcaemia), mucocutaneous candidiasis and Addison disease, which is the opposite of this picture.

medqa-us4-test-0004.why: Itchy, watery eyes with sneezing that recur each spring, and normal acuity, pupils and anterior chamber, point to seasonal allergic conjunctivitis. First-line treatment is a topical antihistamine/mast cell stabiliser such as ketotifen.
notes: Erythromycin ointment treats bacterial conjunctivitis, which gives purulent discharge rather than itch, watery discharge and sneezing.
Warm compresses are for blepharitis, chalazion or meibomian gland dysfunction. Cool compresses may ease allergic symptoms, but they do not treat the allergy.
A topical corticosteroid can raise intraocular pressure and cause cataract. It is kept for severe allergic eye disease that does not respond to first-line drugs, under ophthalmology care.

medqa-us4-test-0007.why: After acute coronary syndrome treated with PCI, the patient needs dual antiplatelet therapy: aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor, usually for 12 months. In Australian ACS guidelines, ticagrelor or prasugrel is generally preferred over clopidogrel unless bleeding risk or contraindications apply.
notes: Short-acting dihydropyridines such as nifedipine cause reflex tachycardia and are linked to worse outcomes after ACS. They play no part in secondary prevention here.
Enoxaparin is used acutely around the ACS and PCI. It is not continued as a discharge medication.
Spironolactone is indicated after MI when LVEF is 40% or less with heart failure or diabetes. This patient's EF of 58% is preserved.

medqa-us4-test-0047.why: Calf claudication with palpable femoral pulses but absent pedal pulses places the stenosis below the femoral artery and above the calf, in the femoropopliteal segment. Pallor and pain on raising the leg (positive Buerger elevation sign) confirm arterial insufficiency in a smoker with diabetes.
notes: Popliteal vein thrombosis causes constant calf swelling and pain. It does not cause exertional cramping that settles with rest, pallor on elevation, or absent pulses.
Lumbar spinal stenosis causes back and leg pain that comes on with standing and eases with flexion, and pulses are normal. Here there is no back pain and pedal pulses are absent.
Aortoiliac disease causes buttock and thigh claudication, weak femoral pulses and erectile dysfunction (Leriche syndrome). This patient's femoral pulses are palpable.

medqa-us4-test-0051.why: Hypertension resistant to three drugs, together with hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis (HCO3 33) despite an ACE inhibitor that should raise potassium, points to primary hyperaldosteronism. Screen with the aldosterone-to-renin ratio.
notes: A phaeochromocytoma causes episodic headache, sweating and palpitations with labile blood pressure, not hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis as the main finding; his pulse is 70.
Cortisol excess can cause hypokalaemia and hypertension, but there are no Cushingoid features, and glucose of 129 alone does not suggest it.
Renal artery stenosis causes secondary hyperaldosteronism, but he has no bruit, no flash pulmonary oedema and a normal BUN; primary aldosteronism is the more common cause of this picture.

medqa-us4-test-0067.why: Fever, tachycardia, irritability, sweating, poor weight gain and a goitre point to neonatal thyrotoxicosis. Maternal TSH receptor-stimulating antibodies cross the placenta and stay in her circulation after thyroidectomy, even though she now needs thyroxine.
notes: Thyroid peroxidase antibodies do not stimulate the thyroid. They do not cause neonatal hyperthyroidism or goitre.
Congenital viral infection gives TORCH features such as rash, hepatosplenomegaly or microcephaly. It does not cause a hyperthyroid picture with goitre.
Neonatal opioid withdrawal causes irritability and sweating, usually starting within the first few days. It does not cause a goitre, and nothing in the history suggests maternal opioid use.

medqa-us4-test-0074.why: An itchy, hypopigmented rash on the upper trunk after heat, humidity and sweating is pityriasis versicolor (Malassezia). KOH preparation confirms it by showing short hyphae and yeast cells, the 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance.
notes: Wood lamp may show yellow-green fluorescence, which supports the diagnosis, but it is often negative and is not confirmatory.
Malassezia is lipophilic and needs special media to grow. Culture is not used to diagnose pityriasis versicolor.
Skin biopsy is invasive and unnecessary when a bedside KOH scraping makes the diagnosis.

medqa-us4-test-0076.why: A firm, fixed vaginal wall mass with postmenopausal bleeding must be treated as possible vaginal cancer. A visible lesion needs tissue diagnosis by biopsy.
notes: Cytology is a screening test and is not used to assess a visible mass. In Australia the Pap smear has also been replaced by HPV-based cervical screening.
Incision and drainage suits a fluctuant, tender abscess or cyst. A firm, immobile mass in a postmenopausal woman needs malignancy excluded first.
Gonorrhoea and chlamydia testing does not explain a firm fixed mass. The urgency is more likely from mass effect on the urethra or bladder.

medqa-us4-test-0084.why: Infertility, recurrent pelvic pain and painful bowel movements around menstruation (dyschezia), with a partner of normal fertility and a normal HSG, suggest endometriosis: endometrial tissue outside the uterus. A normal pelvic examination does not exclude it, and laparoscopy confirms it.
notes: Tubal damage after infection would usually show on the hysterosalpingogram, which was normal, and would not explain cyclic dyschezia.
Fibroids cause heavy menstrual bleeding and an enlarged, irregular uterus on bimanual examination; her examination was normal.
Raised androgens and LH (PCOS) cause irregular cycles and hyperandrogenism, but her cycles are regular at 29 days and there is no hirsutism or acne.

medqa-us4-test-0088.why: A high-speed deceleration injury plus a widened mediastinum, NG tube pushed to the right, a depressed left mainstem bronchus and an upper rib fracture is the classic x-ray picture of traumatic aortic rupture. Blood around the rupture causes the left haemothorax and hypotension. Confirm with CT angiography.
notes: Diaphragmatic rupture shows bowel or the NG tube in the left chest and a raised or blurred hemidiaphragm, not a widened mediastinum with the bronchus pushed down.
Bronchial rupture causes pneumothorax with a persistent air leak, pneumomediastinum and the fallen lung sign; it does not explain a widened mediastinum or the NG tube shifted right.
Tension pneumothorax gives hyperresonance and a mediastinal shift away from the affected side, not dullness at the base; it is treated on clinical signs without waiting for an x-ray.

medqa-us4-test-0108.why: An obese adolescent with hip, groin or knee pain, limited hip movement and inability to bear weight has a slipped capital femoral epiphysis until proven otherwise. An unstable slip needs urgent surgical in situ screw fixation of the epiphysis, with no weight bearing beforehand, to prevent further slip and avascular necrosis.
notes: Casting and crutches do not stabilise the physis, and the slip can progress, so this is not definitive treatment for SCFE.
A Pavlik harness treats developmental dysplasia of the hip in infants under about 6 months, not an adolescent with a slipped epiphysis.
Observation suits transient synovitis or early Legg-Calve-Perthes disease; leaving SCFE untreated risks further slip and avascular necrosis.

medqa-us4-test-0138.why: This is primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis: dry by day, never dry at night, normal examination, normal urinalysis and culture, and well-concentrated morning urine. Management starts with reassurance and an enuresis alarm, which has the best long-term cure rate. Desmopressin is the other first-line option.
notes: Spinal MRI is for suspected occult spinal dysraphism, such as abnormal neurological signs, daytime symptoms or a sacral skin lesion, and none of these is present.
Oxybutynin is for overactive bladder with daytime urgency or frequency; it is not first-line for monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis.
Imipramine works but is third-line because of cardiotoxicity and danger in overdose, so it is kept for cases where alarm and desmopressin have failed.

medqa-us4-test-0144.why: Delayed bone age (11 years at age 14), puberty that has begun (Tanner 2 breasts), normal birth weight and a father who was short as a teenager all point to constitutional delay of growth and puberty. Reassurance and follow-up is the right step.
notes: A pelvic ultrasound would be used for primary amenorrhoea or suspected gonadal dysgenesis, but she has begun puberty and has no Turner features.
DHEA is measured for premature adrenarche or androgen excess, which does not fit delayed growth with absent pubic hair in a constitutionally delayed girl.
Brain MRI is for suspected pituitary or hypothalamic disease, such as headaches, visual field loss or stalled puberty, and none of these is present.

medqa-us4-test-0150.why: Atypical pneumonia with diarrhoea, hyponatraemia and relative bradycardia for the fever suggests Legionella. It needs a respiratory fluoroquinolone or a macrolide. In Australia, guidelines prefer IV azithromycin for suspected Legionella, with ciprofloxacin or moxifloxacin as alternatives.
notes: Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole is first-line for Pneumocystis pneumonia, which needs an immunocompromised host; it is not reliable against Legionella.
Amoxicillin covers Streptococcus pneumoniae, but beta-lactams do not reach intracellular organisms such as Legionella.
Rifampin is not used alone because resistance develops quickly; at most it is an add-on in severe Legionella, never monotherapy.

medqa-us4-test-0154.why: An itchy generalised rash with lesions at different stages at once (macules, papules, vesicles and crusts) on the face, trunk and limbs, after a mild prodrome in a child at daycare, is varicella.
notes: Measles gives a non-itchy maculopapular rash spreading from the head down, with cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and Koplik spots, not vesicles and crusts.
Poison ivy (urushiol) dermatitis forms linear vesicles on exposed skin where the plant touched; it does not cause fever, headache, myalgia or a truncal rash.
Rubella causes a mild pink maculopapular rash spreading from the face down, with postauricular and suboccipital lymphadenopathy, not vesicles; there is no lymphadenopathy here.

medqa-us4-test-0172.why: Acute fluctuating confusion with hallucinations in an older inpatient with sepsis is delirium. Treat the cause and use non-drug measures first. When agitation endangers the patient or staff, a low-dose antipsychotic is preferred; in Australia, haloperidol or risperidone are often used.
notes: Diphenhydramine is strongly anticholinergic and can cause or worsen delirium in older people (Beers criteria).
Benzodiazepines such as lorazepam worsen delirium and increase falls in older people; they are kept for alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal.
Physical restraints increase agitation, injury and delirium; they are a last resort, not the next step when safer drug options exist.

medqa-us4-test-0184.why: Subacute memory and concentration problems with anhedonia, poor sleep, withdrawal, psychomotor slowing and blunted affect, in a patient worried about his own memory, suggest pseudodementia (depression). The deficits improve once the depression is treated, so an SSRI is appropriate.
notes: Aspirin is for vascular disease, but vascular dementia would usually show stepwise decline and focal neurological signs, which are absent here.
A VP shunt treats normal pressure hydrocephalus, which presents with gait disturbance and urinary incontinence alongside dementia, and neither is described.
Memantine is for moderate to severe Alzheimer disease, which develops over years with little insight, not over 5 weeks with prominent depressive symptoms.

medqa-us4-test-0185.why: Intermediate-risk neuroblastoma has a good chance of cure with standard treatment, and refusing it puts the child at serious risk. Parents cannot refuse life-saving treatment for a minor, so the physician should seek a court order. In Australia, this means a Supreme Court (parens patriae) or child protection application.
notes: Arranging home supportive care would accept a refusal that leaves the child with a likely fatal but treatable cancer, so it fails the physician's duty to the child.
Another oncologist would recommend the same standard treatment, so referral delays care without changing anything.
The parents have already refused after a full discussion, and a 2-week delay in a growing malignancy risks making the tumour unresectable.

medqa-us4-test-0190.why: He has recurrent unexpected panic attacks, worry about having more, and avoidance of public places. This is panic disorder with agoraphobia. An SSRI such as citalopram is the first-line long-term medication, usually combined with CBT, which matches Australian guidance.
notes: Lithium is a mood stabiliser for bipolar disorder and has no role in panic disorder.
Propranolol can blunt the physical symptoms of performance anxiety, but it does not prevent panic attacks or treat agoraphobic avoidance over the long term.
Quetiapine is an antipsychotic with metabolic side effects and is not a recommended long-term treatment for panic disorder.

medqa-us4-test-0217.why: A dilated os with a nonviable embryo means an inevitable or incomplete miscarriage. Her tachycardia and hypotension show haemodynamic instability. An unstable patient needs urgent surgical evacuation of the uterus (D&C, called suction curettage in Australia), not medical or expectant management.
notes: Misoprostol is an option for a stable patient with miscarriage, but it works slowly and unpredictably and is not suitable when she is hypotensive and bleeding.
Methotrexate treats a stable ectopic pregnancy, but this is an intrauterine embryo with a dilated os.
Bed rest does not prevent or treat miscarriage, and it does nothing for a nonviable pregnancy with haemodynamic compromise.

medqa-us4-test-0223.why: Her pain starts with menses in a regular cycle a few years after menarche, the exam is normal, and NSAIDs help. This is primary dysmenorrhoea, caused by prostaglandin-driven uterine contractions and ischaemia during endometrial shedding.
notes: PID would cause fever, cervical motion tenderness or discharge and pain not tied to the cycle, and her exam is normal despite her risk factors.
An ovarian cyst does not reliably cause pain that recurs with every period, and adnexal findings would be expected.
Fibroids are rare in adolescents and usually cause heavy bleeding and an enlarged uterus, which she does not have.

medqa-us4-test-0273.why: Years of heavy drinking with recurrent postprandial epigastric pain, steatorrhoea and weight loss suggest chronic pancreatitis, while smoking and weight loss also raise concern for pancreatic cancer. Contrast CT is the first-line test: it shows calcifications, duct changes and any mass.
notes: Endoscopic ultrasound is more invasive and is used when CT is equivocal or a mass needs biopsy, not as the first test.
Ultrasound often shows the pancreas poorly because of bowel gas and is less sensitive for calcifications and masses.
Upper endoscopy looks at the oesophagus, stomach and duodenum, but steatorrhoea and weight loss point to the pancreas, which endoscopy cannot assess.

medqa-us4-test-0280.why: He has a long-standing, irrational fear of flying that causes avoidance and impairs his life. This is a specific phobia. CBT with exposure therapy is the treatment of choice and gives lasting benefit.
notes: A benzodiazepine may be used occasionally before an unavoidable flight, but it does not treat the phobia and can cause dependence.
SSRIs are first line for generalised and social anxiety disorders, but they are not effective first-line treatment for specific phobia.
Psychodynamic therapy is not an evidence-based first-line treatment for specific phobia compared with exposure-based CBT.

medqa-us4-test-0283.why: A viral illness that improved and then worsened, followed by high fever, purulent sputum, leucocytosis and a lobar infiltrate, fits a secondary bacterial pneumonia. S. pneumoniae is the most common cause of typical lobar community-acquired pneumonia, including after influenza.
notes: Mycoplasma causes atypical pneumonia, with dry cough, a gradual onset and patchy interstitial infiltrates, rather than purulent sputum and lobar consolidation.
Chlamydophila causes a mild atypical pneumonia, often with hoarseness and a dry cough, not acute lobar pneumonia with green sputum.
H. influenzae can cause pneumonia, usually in COPD or older patients, but it is much less common than pneumococcus in an otherwise healthy teenager.

medqa-us4-test-0316.why: Her history of bulimia (binge eating and purging) is a contraindication to bupropion, which lowers the seizure threshold, especially with electrolyte disturbance. In Australia, bupropion is approved only for smoking cessation, not depression.
notes: Citalopram is a reasonable first-line SSRI for major depression and is not contraindicated by a history of eating disorder.
Fluoxetine is safe here and is actually the SSRI approved for bulimia nervosa.
Trazodone does not carry the seizure risk of bupropion and can help her insomnia, so it does not need to be avoided.

medqa-us4-test-0324.why: Fever, jaundice and RUQ pain plus hypotension and confusion (Reynolds pentad), with a dilated common bile duct, is acute suppurative cholangitis. Once resuscitated and on antibiotics, he needs urgent biliary drainage, and ERCP is first line. In Australia, noradrenaline rather than dopamine is the usual first vasopressor.
notes: MRCP only images the duct and cannot drain it; ultrasound has already shown obstruction, so MRCP would just delay decompression in a septic patient.
Percutaneous transhepatic drainage is the fallback when ERCP fails, is unavailable, or anatomy is altered; it is not the first choice here.
CT adds little once ultrasound shows a dilated duct in clinical cholangitis, and it delays the drainage this patient needs.

medqa-us4-test-0326.why: A patient with sarcoidosis on treatment is presumably taking corticosteroids, and new groin pain with preserved hip range of motion suggests early avascular necrosis of the femoral head. MRI is the most sensitive test and shows marrow oedema before any change appears on X-ray.
notes: Plain X-rays are often normal early in avascular necrosis and only show sclerosis, crescent sign or collapse later, so they are a poor test for sensitivity.
A bone scan can pick up avascular necrosis but is less sensitive and less specific than MRI, and it has largely been replaced by MRI.
Ultrasound can show a hip effusion but cannot assess the bone marrow, so it cannot diagnose avascular necrosis.

medqa-us4-test-0333.why: His GCS is 8 (eyes open to pain 2, groans 2, withdraws 4) and he has a slow respiratory rate of 10/min, so he cannot protect his airway. Airway comes first in the primary survey: GCS 8 or less means intubate.
notes: Decreased right basal breath sounds may mean a haemothorax that needs drainage, but this is the breathing step and comes after securing the airway in a patient with GCS 8.
Head and neck CT is needed for his likely brain injury, but only once the airway is secured; you never send an unprotected, obtunded patient to the scanner.
Imaging the limb injuries is part of the secondary survey and does not address the immediate threat to his airway.

medqa-us4-test-0361.why: The mother has Graves' disease, so her TSH-receptor antibodies cross the placenta and can cause neonatal thyrotoxicosis. It often appears around day 5-7, once the PTU has cleared from the baby. Here it shows as tachycardia, irritability, frequent stools, weight loss and goitre. Treat with a thionamide plus a beta-blocker. Australian practice may use carbimazole, which is converted to methimazole.
notes: Iodide can be added for a severe thyroid storm, but only after a thionamide has been started; on its own it is not the first-line step.
Naloxone reverses acute opioid toxicity, which causes depressed breathing. Heroin withdrawal causes irritability and loose stools but not a goitre, and naloxone would make withdrawal worse.
Calcium gluconate treats neonatal hypocalcaemia, which causes jitteriness or seizures. It does not explain the goitre, the very fast heart rate or the maternal Graves' history.

medqa-us4-test-0371.why: Massive splenomegaly, pancytopenia, a dry tap on marrow aspiration, lymphocytes with hair-like projections and CD25 positivity point to hairy cell leukaemia. The purine analogue cladribine is first line and gives durable complete remissions in most patients.
notes: Fludarabine is a purine analogue with some activity in hairy cell leukaemia, but it is less effective than cladribine and is mainly used for CLL.
Corticosteroids do not treat hairy cell leukaemia and would make the infection risk from neutropenia worse.
Thalidomide is used for multiple myeloma and has no role in hairy cell leukaemia.

medqa-us4-test-0377.why: She is pregnant, recently returned from Sudan where hepatitis E is endemic, and has acute hepatitis with liver failure (encephalopathy, INR 2.0). This picture points to hepatitis E, which is spread by the faecal-oral route and is fulminant in pregnancy, especially in the third trimester. Anti-HEV IgM confirms acute infection.
notes: Her immunisations are up to date, so she is protected against hepatitis B. The travel history and pregnancy point to HEV, not HBV.
Anti-HAV IgG shows past infection or vaccination, not acute illness. Acute hepatitis A would need IgM, and she is immunised anyway.
She has no risk factors for HCV such as blood products or injecting drugs, HCV rarely causes acute fulminant hepatitis, and IgG does not show acute infection.

medqa-us4-test-0379.why: After a viral illness he has pleuritic chest pain that changes with position (pericarditis). He now has hypotension, raised JVP and pulsus paradoxus, with a systolic drop of 21 mmHg on inspiration. That is cardiac tamponade from a pericardial effusion.
notes: Dilated cardiomyopathy causes heart failure with a displaced apex and an S3, not positional pleuritic pain or a large pulsus paradoxus.
Myocardial infarction causes pressure-like chest pain that does not change with posture, and on its own it does not give pulsus paradoxus after a viral prodrome.
Constrictive pericarditis develops over months and typically shows Kussmaul's sign and a pericardial knock, not acute pulsus paradoxus within days of acute pericarditis.

medqa-us4-test-0383.why: An infant with chronic diarrhoea, failure to thrive, recurrent infections, oral thrush and an absent thymic shadow has severe combined immunodeficiency. The rash may be graft-versus-host disease from maternal T cells. The definitive cure for SCID is haematopoietic stem cell transplantation.
notes: IVIG replaces antibodies and is a supportive bridge, but it does not restore T-cell function, so it cannot cure SCID.
Leucovorin is used for folate antagonist toxicity or certain folate disorders. It does not correct a combined T- and B-cell defect.
Thymic transplantation is used for complete DiGeorge syndrome. That would also feature hypocalcaemia, heart defects and facial features, and most SCID is a stem-cell defect, not a thymic one.

medqa-us4-test-0388.why: A thriving, developmentally normal 8-week-old with effortless regurgitation who settles quickly and keeps growing along his percentiles has physiological gastro-oesophageal reflux (a happy spitter). It resolves on its own, so management is reassurance, upright positioning after feeds and avoiding overfeeding.
notes: PPIs are not indicated for uncomplicated infant reflux without poor weight gain, feeding refusal or oesophagitis, and they carry risks.
Ultrasound is used for suspected pyloric stenosis, which causes projectile, non-bilious vomiting and poor weight gain, not this effortless spitting in a growing baby.
Cutting cow's milk from the mother's diet is for suspected cow's milk protein allergy, which usually comes with blood in the stool, diarrhoea, eczema or poor growth; none are present.

medqa-us4-test-0395.why: Using a reliever more than twice a week and waking at night several times a month means persistent (not intermittent) asthma, so he needs a daily low-dose inhaled corticosteroid. In Australia, children aged 6 to 11 are likewise stepped up to regular low-dose ICS.
notes: Needing a reliever four times a week, waking at night and having limited activity show poorly controlled persistent asthma, so continuing SABA alone is not adequate.
A LABA must never be used as monotherapy in asthma because of increased risk of severe exacerbation and death; it is only added to an ICS at a higher step.
Zileuton is a 5-lipoxygenase inhibitor that is not first-line, needs liver monitoring and is not approved for a 6-year-old; it is also not available in Australia.

medqa-us4-test-0411.why: Intensely itchy grouped vesicles on the buttocks are dermatitis herpetiformis. Together with iron deficiency, chronic diarrhoea, short stature and a raised IgA tTG, this points to coeliac disease, where IgA antibodies against epidermal transglutaminase are deposited in the dermal papillae.
notes: Crohn's disease can cause iron deficiency and poor growth, but its skin signs are erythema nodosum or pyoderma gangrenosum, and it does not raise IgA tTG or cause dermatitis herpetiformis.
CVID causes low immunoglobulins and recurrent sinopulmonary infections; she has a high IgA tTG, and a true IgA deficiency would make that test falsely low.
HSP causes palpable purpura on the buttocks and legs with abdominal pain, arthritis and nephritis; the lesions are not intensely itchy and tTG is not raised.

medqa-us4-test-0414.why: Watery diarrhoea and cramps starting 1 to 3 days after a stay in India, with no fever and no blood, is classic traveller's diarrhoea, and ETEC is the most common cause. Acid suppression with ranitidine also raises the risk. (Ranitidine has been withdrawn in Australia.)
notes: Giardia has a longer incubation period of 1 to 2 weeks and causes greasy, foul-smelling stools with bloating, not acute watery diarrhoea beginning on the trip home.
Shigella causes fever and bloody, mucoid stools with tenesmus, but she has no fever and her stools are watery.
Staphylococcal food poisoning comes 1 to 6 hours after the meal, mostly as vomiting, and settles within a day; her nausea started before the meal and she has been unwell for 3 days.

medqa-us4-test-0419.why: Painful purpura, haemorrhagic bullae and necrosis in fatty areas (thighs, buttocks, penis) a few days after starting warfarin point to warfarin-induced skin necrosis. Protein C falls faster than the clotting factors and causes a temporary hypercoagulable state. Treat by stopping warfarin, giving vitamin K and heparin, and replacing protein C.
notes: Hyperbaric oxygen is used for necrotising soft tissue infection or carbon monoxide poisoning; it does not correct the protein C deficiency that causes this necrosis.
Argatroban is a direct thrombin inhibitor used for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia; this patient has had no heparin and his problem is caused by warfarin.
Tranexamic acid blocks fibrinolysis and would make the microvascular thrombosis behind this necrosis worse.

medqa-us4-test-0428.why: Painful vesicles on the fingertip pulp of a dental worker exposed to oral secretions is herpetic whitlow from HSV. It is treated with supportive care plus oral acyclovir, especially early in the illness. Incision and drainage is avoided.
notes: Cephalexin treats a bacterial felon or paronychia, which present with a tense, purulent pulp abscess rather than clustered clear vesicles, and the mild leucocytosis does not change that.
Smoking cessation is advisable generally and for thromboangiitis obliterans risk, but it is a distractor here: Buerger disease causes ischaemic digits, not acute vesicles.
Washing is for poison oak contact dermatitis, which causes itchy, linear vesicles 1 to 2 days after exposure, not a single painful, swollen finger pulp a week later.

medqa-us4-test-0432.why: Confusion, nystagmus (ophthalmoplegia) and ataxia in a person with alcohol use disorder is Wernicke encephalopathy. Give IV thiamine immediately, and before any glucose, to prevent progression to Korsakoff syndrome.
notes: Naltrexone helps maintain abstinence once the patient is stable, but it does nothing for acute Wernicke encephalopathy.
The macrocytosis may reflect alcohol use or folate or B12 deficiency, but B12 deficiency does not explain the acute triad, and thiamine is the urgent priority.
Giving glucose before thiamine can precipitate or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy; check glucose, but give thiamine first.

medqa-us4-test-0434.why: Slowly worsening memory loss over years, getting lost, being unaware of his deficits and needing help with daily tasks fit Alzheimer disease. First-line drug treatment is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor such as donepezil, which raises cholinergic signalling.
notes: Drugs that enhance GABA, such as benzodiazepines, worsen confusion and raise fall risk in older people with dementia; they do not treat Alzheimer disease.
Dopaminergic drugs treat Parkinson disease; he has no tremor, rigidity or bradykinesia.
Memantine, an NMDA glutamate antagonist, is used for moderate to severe disease, either added to or after a cholinesterase inhibitor; it is not the usual first drug.

medqa-us4-test-0460.why: A painless, solid testicular mass that does not transilluminate, together with gynecomastia, points to a Leydig cell tumor. These tumors secrete estrogen, or androgens that are aromatised to estrogen. Gynecomastia that began 18 months ago also came before the injury 3 months ago.
notes: Obesity can cause gynecomastia through peripheral aromatisation, but it does not explain a solid intratesticular mass.
Klinefelter syndrome gives small, firm testes, tall stature and infertility, not a discrete 1.5-cm testicular mass in a man of average height.

The injury happened 3 months ago, but the gynecomastia started 18 months ago. A post-traumatic haematoma would usually be tender. The injury most likely just drew attention to a tumour that was already there.

medqa-us4-test-0475.why: He has a fast, irregular tachyarrhythmia (likely atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response) with hypotension and chest pain, so he is haemodynamically unstable. Unstable tachyarrhythmias need immediate synchronised cardioversion.
notes: Angiography may be needed later for ischaemia, but the unstable rhythm and hypotension must be corrected first.
Esmolol is a beta-blocker that lowers blood pressure and would worsen his shock at 85/55 mm Hg; rate control suits stable patients.
Amiodarone is for haemodynamically stable patients or after cardioversion fails; it works too slowly for a patient who is hypotensive with chest pain.

medqa-us4-test-0504.why: Bilateral retracted, immobile eardrums show chronic otitis media with effusion lasting at least 3 months. With hearing loss and speech delay, he needs tympanostomy tubes (grommets).
notes: Adenoidectomy is not first-line in children under 4 unless there is marked nasal obstruction; it is usually added if tubes need to be reinserted, and his adenoids are only mildly enlarged.
Antihistamines do not resolve otitis media with effusion and are not recommended.
Oral or intranasal steroids give no lasting benefit in otitis media with effusion and are not recommended.

medqa-us4-test-0507.why: He has severe pneumonia with septic shock, gram-negative rods on Gram stain and Pseudomonas risk factors: COPD, repeated antibiotics and steroids, and chemotherapy. He needs an antipseudomonal beta-lactam plus atypical cover with a fluoroquinolone. In Australia, piperacillin-tazobactam plus azithromycin is commonly used.
notes: Ceftriaxone and azithromycin cover standard community-acquired pneumonia organisms but not Pseudomonas, which his risk factors make likely.
Ertapenem lacks activity against Pseudomonas and Acinetobacter, so it is not suitable empirical cover for this patient.
Colistin is a last-line drug kept for multidrug or carbapenem-resistant gram-negative infection; it is nephrotoxic and has no role as first empirical therapy.

medqa-us4-test-0511.why: Episodes of left-hand weakness and numbness are transient ischaemic attacks in the right carotid territory, and he has a right carotid bruit. Carotid duplex ultrasound is the first-line, non-invasive test for symptomatic carotid stenosis, which may need endarterectomy before his elective surgery.
notes: Echocardiography looks for a cardioembolic source, but nothing points to one here (no murmur, sinus rhythm), and the bruit with same-territory symptoms points to the carotid first.
Anticoagulation is for cardioembolic sources such as atrial fibrillation; large-artery atherosclerotic TIA is treated with antiplatelets, statin and possibly revascularisation, not warfarin.
CT angiography of the head looks at intracranial vessels and would miss the main lesion here, which is cervical carotid stenosis; carotid duplex is the first-line test.

medqa-us4-test-0513.why: Leg numbness and weakness brought on by walking and relieved by leaning forward (cycling, pushing a shopping trolley) is neurogenic claudication. Spinal flexion widens the canal, and this is classic for lumbar spinal stenosis in an older adult.
notes: Osteoporosis makes a compression fracture possible, but it would cause focal midline spinal tenderness and would not explain exertional leg symptoms that ease with flexion.

Disc herniation usually affects younger adults, causes radicular pain that gets worse with flexion and sitting, and gives a positive straight-leg raise. It does not cause walking-induced symptoms that ease when leaning forward.
Muscle strain causes localised pain and stiffness, often with paraspinal tenderness, and would not cause leg numbness and weakness linked to walking and posture.

medqa-us4-test-0514.why: Recurrent sinopulmonary infections plus chronic giardiasis (pear-shaped flagellates) suggest selective IgA deficiency. These patients can make anti-IgA antibodies and have anaphylaxis to blood products that contain IgA. In Australia, washed components or products from IgA-deficient donors are arranged through Lifeblood.
notes: Cutaneous and visceral granulomas are seen in chronic granulomatous disease, which presents with catalase-positive bacterial and fungal abscesses, not giardiasis and sinusitis.
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma risk is higher in common variable immunodeficiency and Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome; in IgA deficiency the more classic exam association is transfusion anaphylaxis.
Disseminated mycobacterial infection points to IFN-gamma/IL-12 axis defects or T-cell deficiency, not an isolated humoral IgA defect.

medqa-us4-test-0519.why: A gunshot wound below the nipple line (6th intercostal space) is thoracoabdominal and likely to have crossed the diaphragm into the abdomen, probably injuring the liver. With persistent hypotension and abdominal tenderness, a haemodynamically unstable penetrating injury needs immediate laparotomy, not more imaging.
notes: CT is for haemodynamically stable patients; sending a hypotensive trauma patient to the scanner delays definitive haemorrhage control.
Local wound exploration is sometimes used for stable anterior abdominal stab wounds; it is not appropriate for a gunshot wound in an unstable patient.
VATS is for stable patients, for example to assess the diaphragm or evacuate a retained haemothorax; the shock and abdominal findings here call for laparotomy.

medqa-us4-test-0522.why: Colicky pain, bilious vomiting, obstipation, distension and high-pitched bowel sounds point to mechanical small bowel obstruction. In a patient with previous appendectomy and laparoscopic scars, the likely cause is adhesions. Remember that adhesions are the most common cause of small bowel obstruction in adults.
notes: Psoriasis is not inflammatory bowel disease, and nothing in his history (no diarrhoea, bleeding or weight loss) suggests Crohn stricturing.
Ibuprofen can cause ulcers and, rarely, diaphragm-like strictures, but adhesions after previous surgery are a far more likely cause of obstruction.
Two beers a day explains the mildly raised GGT, but alcohol does not cause mechanical small bowel obstruction.

medqa-us4-test-0532.why: A new drug started 10 days ago plus hypothermia after cold exposure, bradycardia, slowed breathing and paradoxical undressing points to an antipsychotic. Fluphenazine, a typical antipsychotic used here for schizoaffective disorder, disrupts hypothalamic temperature control through dopamine blockade. Antipsychotics can cause hypothermia as well as hyperthermia.
notes: Lisinopril can cause angioedema, cough, hyperkalaemia or hypotension, but it does not disrupt temperature control. His blood pressure is also normal.
Levothyroxine treats hypothyroidism and would protect against hypothermia. Too much of it causes thyrotoxic features such as tachycardia and heat intolerance, not this picture.
Atorvastatin can cause myopathy or rhabdomyolysis, but not hypothermia, altered mental status or paradoxical undressing.

medqa-us4-test-0542.why: A raised maternal serum AFP on its own (here 3 times the median, well above the usual 2-2.5 cut-off) with normal hCG, estriol and inhibin A suggests an open neural tube defect. Other causes include abdominal wall defects, multiple pregnancy or wrong dates. The next step is a detailed ultrasound.
notes: A partial mole raises beta-hCG markedly and does not cause an isolated rise in AFP. Here the hCG is normal.
Trisomy 18 lowers AFP, hCG and estriol, with normal inhibin A. This patient's AFP is high.
Trisomy 21 gives low AFP, low estriol, high hCG and high inhibin A, which is the opposite of this isolated raised AFP.

medqa-us4-test-0547.why: This is an acute focal deficit within the thrombolysis window. The urgent first step is non-contrast head CT to rule out haemorrhage before reperfusion therapy. In Australia this is usually done with CT angiography and perfusion as one stroke protocol.
notes: MRI is more sensitive for early ischaemia but takes longer and is less available, so it should not hold up the decision on thrombolysis.
Lumbar puncture has no place in focal stroke assessment and is only considered when CT is negative and subarachnoid haemorrhage is suspected.
The carotid bruit justifies carotid imaging later, but it comes after haemorrhage has been excluded and acute treatment decided.

medqa-us4-test-0552.why: She has acute cholangitis: fever, jaundice, right upper quadrant pain and dilated ducts with gallstones. Despite antibiotics she now has new confusion and a rising pulse, a progression toward Reynolds pentad. She needs urgent biliary drainage, and ERCP is first-line because it both diagnoses and treats.
notes: Cholecystectomy removes the gallbladder but does not drain the blocked common bile duct. It is done electively once the cholangitis has resolved.
MRCP only images the ducts and cannot drain them. Ultrasound has already shown duct dilatation, and she is getting worse, so a test that cannot treat would only delay care.

Percutaneous cholecystostomy drains the gallbladder in high-risk acute cholecystitis. It does not relieve a blocked common bile duct. If ERCP fails, the alternative is percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage.

medqa-us4-test-0571.why: High fever, productive cough, pleuritic pain and focal crackles at the right base on day 3 after upper abdominal surgery point to pneumonia. Smoking, obesity and splinting from an upper abdominal incision all raise the risk.
notes: Pulmonary embolism can cause pleuritic pain, but high fever with productive cough and crackles fits infection better. Normal breathing rate and heart rate also make PE less likely.
A subphrenic abscess usually appears 1–2 weeks after surgery, and her abdomen is soft and nontender.
A pneumothorax causes sudden breathlessness and reduced breath sounds, not fever, sputum or crackles.

medqa-us4-test-0605.why: Conjunctival injection, dry mouth, tachycardia, anxiety and slowed thinking at a social event are classic signs of cannabis intoxication. Bloodshot eyes are the key clue that separates it from stimulants.
notes: Alcohol causes disinhibition, slurred speech and an unsteady gait, not bloodshot eyes with a dry mouth and anxiety.
Cocaine causes dilated pupils, hypertension, agitation and sometimes chest pain. His blood pressure is normal and his eyes are bloodshot.
PCP causes nystagmus, violence, high blood pressure and ataxia, none of which he has.

medqa-us4-test-0615.why: Painful twisting of the neck (torticollis), with a sensory trick that relieves it, within days of starting haloperidol is acute dystonia. Treat it with an anticholinergic such as benztropine; diphenhydramine is an alternative.
notes: Physical therapy has no role in acute drug-induced dystonia, which responds quickly to an anticholinergic.
Dantrolene is used for neuroleptic malignant syndrome or malignant hyperthermia. He has no fever, generalised rigidity or altered consciousness.
Baclofen treats spasticity and is not used for acute drug-induced dystonia.

medqa-us4-test-0618.why: He stopped heavy drinking 5 days ago and now has fever, tachycardia, hypertension, tactile hallucinations and disorientation. That is delirium tremens. Benzodiazepines such as diazepam are first-line because they act on the same GABA-A receptor as alcohol, control the withdrawal and prevent seizures and death.
notes: Chlorpromazine is a low-potency antipsychotic. It lowers the seizure threshold and causes hypotension, and it does not treat the GABA deficit behind alcohol withdrawal.
Clonidine can blunt adrenergic signs such as tachycardia and hypertension. It does not prevent seizures or delirium, so at most it is an add-on, never the first treatment for delirium tremens.
Haloperidol may be added for agitation or hallucinations that persist after adequate benzodiazepine dosing. Used alone it lowers the seizure threshold and leaves the withdrawal itself untreated.

medqa-us4-test-0710.why: Envelope-shaped crystals are calcium oxalate. After small bowel resection in Crohn disease, unabsorbed fatty acids bind gut calcium, so free oxalate is absorbed in the colon (enteric hyperoxaluria). Fat malabsorption is the key factor.
notes: Primary hyperparathyroidism does cause calcium stones, but nothing in the stem suggests it (no hypercalcaemia, bone or psychiatric features), whereas the bowel resection explains the stones directly.
Excess vitamin D can cause hypercalciuric stones, but a standard multivitamin is unlikely to cause toxicity, and enteric hyperoxaluria fits the Crohn history better.
A high urine pH favours struvite and calcium phosphate stones. Bowel disease with chronic diarrhoea usually makes urine acidic, and the crystals described are oxalate.

medqa-us4-test-0729.why: A 6-week-old boy with nonbilious projectile vomiting straight after feeds and a palpable epigastric 'olive' has hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Ultrasound shows an elongated, thickened pylorus, and pyloromyotomy is the treatment.
notes: A dilated colon segment suggests Hirschsprung disease, which presents with delayed meconium, constipation and distension, not nonbilious vomiting with an epigastric mass.
Rotavirus gastroenteritis causes vomiting with diarrhoea and often fever, and would not produce a palpable epigastric mass.
A triple bubble suggests jejunal atresia, which gives bilious vomiting in the first days of life. Duodenal atresia, the obstruction linked to Down syndrome, shows a double bubble and is also bilious.

medqa-us4-test-0760.why: This is acute delirium with a fluctuating, evening-worse course, in an older woman on hydrochlorothiazide who has eaten and drunk poorly. Thiazide-induced hyponatraemia is the most likely cause, so checking serum electrolytes is the first step.
notes: Thyroid disease can cause confusion, but it rarely produces an acute delirium over 2 days, and TSH is not the first-line test when a thiazide plus poor intake points to hyponatraemia.
A head CT is for delirium with focal neurological signs, trauma or anticoagulation. With no focal deficits, check for a metabolic cause first, even with remote breast cancer.
A chest x-ray looks for pneumonia, but she has no fever, cough or abnormal vital signs, so infection is less likely than a thiazide-related electrolyte disturbance.

medqa-us4-test-0767.why: A postmenopausal nulliparous woman with early menarche, weight loss, ascites and an adnexal mass most likely has epithelial ovarian cancer. CA-125 is the tumour marker expected to be raised. In Australia, RMI scoring (ultrasound, menopausal status and CA-125) guides referral.
notes: Beta-hCG is raised in pregnancy and some germ cell tumours. Germ cell tumours occur in young women, not a postmenopausal woman of 61.
She has ascites but no signs of chronic liver disease, so a prolonged PT from cirrhosis is unlikely. Malignant ascites from an adnexal mass fits better.
Her earlier ASC-US was HPV-negative, so the risk of cervical dysplasia is low, and dysplasia would not explain an adnexal mass, ascites or weight loss.

medqa-us4-test-0804.why: Descending symmetric weakness starting with cranial nerve signs (blurred vision, dysarthria, dysphagia), with reduced reflexes and no fever, in a man who cans his own food, is foodborne botulism. Give botulinum antitoxin early, plus supportive care.
notes: Neostigmine helps myasthenia gravis, where the problem is too few receptors. In botulism, acetylcholine release is blocked before the synapse, so cholinesterase inhibitors work poorly.
Plasmapheresis treats Guillain-Barré syndrome, which usually causes ascending weakness. The descending pattern with early cranial nerve signs and home-canned food points to botulism.
Riluzole is a disease-modifying treatment for ALS, which progresses over months with mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs, not over 1 to 2 days.

medqa-us4-test-0814.why: A testis that has not come down into the scrotum by 6 months is unlikely to descend on its own. Surgical orchiopexy is recommended between 6 and 18 months of age to protect fertility, lower cancer risk and allow examination of the testis. Australian guidance also advises surgery at around 6-12 months, and by 18 months at the latest.
notes: Hormone therapy with hCG gives poor and often temporary results, and current guidelines do not recommend it for cryptorchidism.
Exploratory laparoscopy is for a testis that cannot be felt. This testis can be felt in the inguinal canal.
Orchiectomy is kept for a nonviable or atrophic testis, or an undescended testis found after puberty. A testis that can be felt at 11 months should be preserved.

medqa-us4-test-0815.why: Low-grade fever, nausea, leukocytosis, raised CRP and right costovertebral angle tenderness in a sexually active young woman point to acute pyelonephritis. The first test is urinalysis, with urine culture, to confirm pyuria and bacteriuria before starting antibiotics.
notes: A cervical swab looks for chlamydia or gonorrhoea, but the abdomen is soft and nontender with no pelvic findings, so flank tenderness suggests a kidney source rather than PID.
Blood cultures are for septic or severely unwell patients; this woman is haemodynamically stable, so they are not the first step.
CT is for complicated pyelonephritis or no response after 48 to 72 hours of antibiotics, and should only be considered after urinalysis confirms the diagnosis.

medqa-us4-test-0819.why: A 46,XY karyotype with complete androgen insensitivity gives normal breasts (testosterone is aromatised to oestrogen), scant axillary and pubic hair, a blind vaginal pouch, no uterus (AMH from the testes is intact) and inguinal testes. Primary amenorrhoea with breasts but no uterus and little hair points to this.
notes: 5-alpha reductase deficiency gives ambiguous or female-looking genitalia at birth that virilise at puberty, and breasts do not develop, so it does not fit normal breasts here.
Mosaicism such as 45,X/46,XY gives variable gonadal dysgenesis, often with Müllerian structures and poor breast development. It does not explain normal breasts with no uterus.
Turner syndrome (45,X) causes short stature and absent breast development from streak ovaries, and the uterus is present. This tall girl has normal breasts and no uterus.

medqa-us4-test-0832.why: Sudden hypoxia, hypotension, confusion and DIC (bleeding, undetectable fibrinogen) during labour after membrane rupture is amniotic fluid embolism. Amniotic fluid enters the maternal circulation through endocervical veins or uterine tears and triggers an anaphylactoid reaction with consumptive coagulopathy.
notes: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy can cause shock and pulmonary oedema, but it does not cause acute DIC with undetectable fibrinogen.
A high or total spinal causes hypotension and bradycardia with ascending block, not tachycardia, hypoxia, crackles and coagulopathy, and it would come on within minutes of the block.
Sepsis can cause DIC, but she is nearly afebrile and the collapse was abrupt; GBS colonisation is a risk to the neonate, not a cause of sudden maternal collapse.

medqa-us4-test-0846.why: Neurological episodes separated in time and space (an earlier leg episode that was worse in heat, the Uhthoff phenomenon, and now an upper motor neuron cervical myelopathy with bladder involvement) suggest multiple sclerosis. MRI of the brain and spine is the key test, showing demyelinating plaques that fulfil the McDonald criteria.
notes: Muscle biopsy is for myopathy; hyperreflexia, spasticity and sensory loss point to the central nervous system, not muscle.
Neurosyphilis is unlikely given the relapsing-remitting course and heat sensitivity, and RPR would not show the lesions that confirm MS.
CSF oligoclonal bands support MS, but lumbar puncture is an adjunct after MRI or when MRI is inconclusive, not the first test.

medqa-us4-test-0848.why: A bite that is painless at first and over hours develops blistering, then a bluish plaque with central necrosis and an erythematous rim (the red, white and blue sign), in the south-central US, is loxoscelism. The cause is the brown recluse spider's sphingomyelinase D venom.
notes: A rattlesnake bite hurts immediately, leaves fang marks with rapid swelling, and often causes coagulopathy; it would not be painless or noticed only as something crawling.
A bark scorpion sting causes immediate pain and neurotoxic features, such as paraesthesias and roving eye movements, without local necrosis; it is also found mainly in Arizona.
Deer tick bites cause Lyme disease with an expanding erythema migrans rash days to weeks later, not necrosis within hours.

medqa-us4-test-0867.why: A young man with an unprovoked DVT and a family history of thrombosis whose aPTT barely rises despite a heparin bolus and infusion has heparin resistance. Heparin works by potentiating antithrombin III, so AT III deficiency is the cause.
notes: Factor V Leiden is the most common inherited thrombophilia, but it does not impair the heparin response, so the aPTT would prolong normally.
Protein C deficiency causes thrombosis and warfarin-induced skin necrosis, but heparin response is preserved.
Antiphospholipid syndrome usually gives a baseline prolonged aPTT from the lupus anticoagulant, whereas here it is normal at 26 seconds; it also does not explain heparin failure.

medqa-us4-test-0886.why: She is a sexually active woman under 25, so she should have yearly chlamydia and gonorrhoea screening even with a normal exam. In Australia, annual chlamydia testing (usually with gonorrhoea) is advised for sexually active people under 30, and cervical screening is a 5-yearly HPV test from age 25, not a Pap smear.
notes: She is on the pill, her periods are regular and her last period was 2 weeks ago, so a routine pregnancy test isn't needed before refilling her contraception.
Her normal cytology was only 2 years ago, and at her age cytology is repeated every 3 years, so it isn't due yet.
Her age and sexual activity mean she needs yearly chlamydia and gonorrhoea screening, so doing nothing misses a recommended test.

medqa-us4-test-0896.why: He has had more than 6 months of bizarre delusions (aliens stealing his thoughts), disorganised thinking, flat affect and social withdrawal, with no substance or medical cause. That meets the criteria for schizophrenia: two or more core symptoms with at least 6 months of disturbance.
notes: Delusional disorder involves non-bizarre delusions with otherwise preserved thinking and function, not disorganised speech and negative symptoms.
There is no depressive or manic episode, and his psychosis is not confined to mood episodes.
Schizoid personality is lifelong detachment without psychosis, whereas he has delusions and thought disorder.

medqa-us4-test-0924.why: She is an obese middle-aged woman whose knee pain gets worse with use. She has brief morning stiffness (under 30 min), crepitus, medial joint-line tenderness and a normal ESR, which points to osteoarthritis. The x-ray finding is osteophytes with asymmetric joint-space narrowing. Her mildly raised uric acid is a distractor.
notes: Mixed lytic and sclerotic lesions suggest metastases or Paget disease, which would cause constant or night pain, not use-related pain with crepitus at the joint line.
Effusion and pannus suggest rheumatoid arthritis, which would show prolonged morning stiffness, symmetric small-joint involvement and a raised ESR.
A fluid-filled pouch is a Baker (popliteal) cyst, which causes a lump at the back of the knee, not anteromedial joint-line tenderness.

medqa-us4-test-0928.why: He stays hypotensive after IM adrenaline and fluids, and he takes labetalol. Beta-blockade blunts the response to adrenaline. Glucagon raises cAMP without going through beta-receptors, so it is the rescue drug for refractory anaphylaxis in a beta-blocked patient.
notes: Dopamine is a pressor that acts partly through beta-receptors, so beta-blockade blunts it too, and it is not the recommended rescue for refractory anaphylaxis on a beta-blocker.
Corticosteroids act slowly and have no proven acute benefit. They will not correct shock that persists after adrenaline.
Noradrenaline can be added for refractory shock, but it does not get around beta-blockade. Glucagon is the step aimed at the labetalol.

medqa-us4-test-0936.why: She is a woman of reproductive age with right-sided lower abdominal pain, so ectopic pregnancy must be excluded first. A beta-hCG decides which imaging is safe and appropriate (ultrasound or CT). Pregnancy testing comes before any imaging in these patients.
notes: A plain abdominal x-ray adds little for suspected appendicitis or ectopic pregnancy, and it uses radiation before pregnancy has been excluded.
CT may later confirm appendicitis, but pregnancy must be excluded before any ionising imaging in a woman of reproductive age.
Stool occult blood does not help with acute right lower quadrant pain and would not change urgent management.

medqa-us4-test-0987.why: He was born at home without newborn screening and has a musty odour, fair skin and blue eyes, eczema, developmental delay and seizures, which points to phenylketonuria. Limiting dietary phenylalanine from early infancy prevents the neurological damage. Australian newborn screening tests for PKU.
notes: Untreated hypothyroidism causes coarse features, a large tongue and hypotonia, not a musty odour with fair hair and skin, and maternal thyroxine wouldn't prevent this.
Allopurinol lowers uric acid in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, which causes self-mutilation and gouty problems, not a musty odour and fair skin.
Avoiding fasting prevents hypoglycaemic crises in fatty acid oxidation defects or glycogen storage disease, which don't cause a musty odour or fair skin.

medqa-us4-test-1007.why: A newborn with delayed meconium, abdominal distension and absent bowel sounds has suspected low bowel obstruction (meconium ileus is likely given his Ashkenazi CF risk). A plain abdominal x-ray comes first to confirm obstruction and look for perforation or free air.
notes: A contrast enema can diagnose and treat meconium ileus or Hirschsprung disease, but it comes after a plain film has excluded perforation.
An upper GI series checks for malrotation or high obstruction, but distension with no meconium points to the lower bowel, and a plain film comes first.
Sweat testing confirms CF later on but isn't reliable in the first days of life and doesn't deal with the acute obstruction.

medqa-us4-test-1008.why: She has no urinary symptoms, no fever, and confusion that matches her known dementia. A positive culture and urinalysis here mean asymptomatic bacteriuria. In older people this is not treated. Treating it is reserved for pregnancy and before urological procedures.
notes: TMP-SMX (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) would treat a symptomatic UTI. Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria gives no benefit and adds adverse effects and resistance.
Nitrofurantoin is a first-line drug for cystitis, but this patient has no symptoms, so no antibiotic is indicated.
Levofloxacin is a poor choice in any case because of tendon, CNS and QT risks in older people, and this bacteriuria needs no treatment at all.

medqa-us4-test-1047.why: A middle-aged woman with itch, cholestatic liver tests (very high ALP) and dry eyes and mouth suggesting Sjögren syndrome most likely has primary biliary cholangitis. PBC causes marked hypercholesterolaemia, which shows up as xanthomas and xanthelasma.
notes: IVC or hepatic vein thrombosis (Budd-Chiari syndrome) causes ascites, pain and hepatomegaly. It is not linked to sicca symptoms or chronic itch.
A raised CA 19-9 points to pancreatic or biliary cancer. Without weight loss or a mass, and with sicca symptoms, autoimmune cholestasis is more likely.
Kayser-Fleischer rings point to Wilson disease, which usually presents before 40 with hepatitis or neuropsychiatric features rather than sicca symptoms.

medqa-us4-test-1084.why: Newborns breathe through the nose. Cyanosis that gets worse with feeding and improves with crying (mouth breathing) is the classic sign of bilateral choanal atresia. It is confirmed when a catheter cannot be passed through the nose into the pharynx.
notes: Reticulogranular densities fit respiratory distress syndrome in preterm infants. This baby was born at term, and crying would not relieve the cyanosis.
A boot-shaped heart fits tetralogy of Fallot. In that condition crying worsens cyanosis (tet spells) rather than relieving it.
Failure to pass a gastric tube through the mouth points to oesophageal atresia. That causes drooling and choking with feeds, not cyanosis that is relieved by crying.

medqa-us4-test-1093.why: She is postmenopausal and has several osteoporosis risk factors: low BMI (18), smoking, heavy alcohol use and Asian ethnicity. That justifies DXA screening before age 65. In Australia, DXA is likewise advised for women under 70 with risk factors.
notes: Her cervical screening 2 years ago was normal, so she isn't due. In Australia she would have a 5-yearly HPV test up to age 74.
AAA ultrasound screening is for men aged 65 to 75 who have ever smoked, not a 62-year-old woman.
A soft S4 in a woman with hypertension and no symptoms reflects a stiff left ventricle and doesn't call for an invasive transoesophageal echo.

medqa-us4-test-1109.why: A CD4 count of 80, subacute headache, confusion and India ink showing encapsulated yeasts point to cryptococcal meningitis. Induction treatment is amphotericin B plus flucytosine for at least 2 weeks, followed by fluconazole consolidation. Liposomal amphotericin is usually preferred.
notes: This regimen treats cerebral toxoplasmosis, which presents with ring-enhancing lesions, not encapsulated yeasts in the CSF.
Fluconazole is used for consolidation and maintenance after induction. On its own it is inferior as initial therapy for cryptococcal meningitis.
This is empirical cover for bacterial meningitis. The CSF here (lymphocytic, mild changes, encapsulated yeasts on India ink) shows a fungal cause.

medqa-us4-test-1116.why: Five months of widespread pain with symmetric tender points, fatigue, poor sleep, paraesthesias and bloating, a normal examination and a normal ESR and TSH all point to fibromyalgia. Besides exercise and education, low-dose amitriptyline at night is first-line drug therapy because it helps both pain and sleep.
notes: Benzodiazepines such as temazepam are not effective for fibromyalgia and carry dependence risk.
A normal MCV and normal reflexes and strength give no reason to suspect B12 deficiency; her tingling is a common fibromyalgia symptom.
A normal ESR and the absence of synovitis argue against inflammatory arthritis, so methotrexate has no role.

medqa-us4-test-1119.why: In an obese woman, pain at the anteromedial proximal tibia a few centimetres below the joint line, worse on stairs and rising from a chair, with no effusion and a stable knee, is classic pes anserine bursitis. Remember the location: below the joint line over the insertion of sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus.
notes: A stress fracture fits repetitive high-impact loading, such as in runners. Normal radiographs with no history of overuse make it less likely.
A meniscal tear causes joint line tenderness, effusion, locking or catching, usually after a twisting injury. None of these is present.
An MCL sprain needs a valgus injury and gives pain or laxity on valgus stress testing, which was negative here.

medqa-us4-test-1121.why: Bilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia (adduction deficit with nystagmus of the abducting eye on each side) in a young woman, with recent imbalance and disc hyperaemia suggesting optic neuritis, points to multiple sclerosis. The cause is demyelination of the MLF.
notes: A pontine tumour would usually cause progressive deficits and cranial nerve palsies. It would be unusual in a 25-year-old with relapsing, multifocal signs and a recent normal CT.
Wernicke encephalopathy happens with malnutrition or alcohol use and gives ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and confusion. Nothing in her history suggests thiamine deficiency.
An INO from brainstem infarction is typically one-sided and occurs in older patients with vascular risk factors, not as bilateral INO in a young woman.

medqa-us4-test-1124.why: Frothy, foul-smelling yellow-green discharge with vulvovaginal erythema, pH above 4.5 and multiple partners is classic trichomoniasis. A wet mount shows motile flagellated protozoa. In Australia, NAAT for Trichomonas vaginalis is now the preferred test.
notes: Gram-negative diplococci indicate gonorrhoea, which mainly causes cervicitis with mucopurulent cervical discharge rather than frothy vaginitis.
A positive whiff test is the hallmark of bacterial vaginosis, which gives thin grey discharge without vulvovaginal inflammation.
Pseudohyphae indicate candidiasis, which is plausible after amoxicillin. However, candida gives thick white discharge with a normal pH below 4.5.

medqa-us4-test-1125.why: Cramping that started once cycles became ovulatory, a normal examination and no other red flags fit primary dysmenorrhoea. NSAIDs, which inhibit prostaglandins, are first-line, with hormonal contraception if they fail. Imaging is reserved for cases that do not respond or have abnormal findings.
notes: Pelvic ultrasound is for suspected secondary dysmenorrhoea (abnormal examination, failure of NSAIDs or hormones). It is not the first step in typical primary dysmenorrhoea.
MRI is a second-line test for anatomical problems such as Mullerian anomalies or adenomyosis. It is not indicated before an empirical NSAID trial.
Exercise may help a little, but she is already active on a soccer team. NSAIDs have the strongest evidence as first-line therapy.

medqa-us4-test-1130.why: Tremor, lid retraction, digital swelling (thyroid acropachy) and tachycardic atrial fibrillation point to Graves hyperthyroidism. A beta-blocker such as propranolol controls the adrenergic symptoms and the ventricular rate while antithyroid treatment is started.
notes: Digoxin works poorly for rate control in the high adrenergic state of thyrotoxicosis. Beta-blockers are preferred.
