notes: Facet joint hypertrophy causes chronic axial pain or spinal stenosis in older patients, not sudden radiculopathy after lifting at age 35.
Osteophytes are degenerative and come on slowly in older patients. They don't explain sudden pain after lifting with a positive straight-leg raise.
Spondylolisthesis causes chronic low back pain, often in athletes or older adults. It is not the usual cause of acute S1 radiculopathy after lifting.

mmlu-professional_medicine-045.why: Diabetes is an indication for yearly influenza vaccination, and October is the start of the Northern Hemisphere flu season. In Australia, influenza vaccine is funded for people with diabetes and is given before winter, from about April.
notes: Her BMI is 20, which is normal. Weight-loss advice is not indicated.
Routine HPV co-testing is not recommended at 22, and her Pap smear was normal 3 months ago. Australia uses 5-yearly HPV cervical screening from age 25.
A grandmother diagnosed at 67 does not make her high risk. Mammography is not indicated for a 22-year-old.

mmlu-professional_medicine-053.why: Cocaine chest pain with severe hypertension that persists despite benzodiazepines and nitrates is driven by alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction. Phentolamine, an alpha-blocker, reverses it. Pure beta-blockers are avoided because they can leave alpha stimulation unopposed.
notes: Carvedilol does block alpha receptors, but its beta-blockade is stronger. It is not the preferred agent in acute cocaine toxicity; a direct alpha-blocker is.
He has no pulmonary oedema or volume overload, and his lungs are clear. A diuretic does not treat cocaine-induced vasospasm.
Metoprolol is a selective beta-blocker. It can cause unopposed alpha vasoconstriction, worsening coronary spasm and hypertension.

mmlu-professional_medicine-059.why: Infant inguinal hernias are indirect (patent processus vaginalis). They do not close spontaneously and carry a high risk of incarceration, especially in the first year. A reducible, uncomplicated hernia should be repaired electively at the earliest convenient time.
notes: Postponing is reasonable for umbilical hernias, which often close by age 4 to 5, but not for inguinal hernias, which persist and risk incarceration while waiting.
Oligospermia is not what drives the timing. The risk is incarceration with bowel or testicular ischaemia, which can happen at any age, so waiting years is inappropriate.
Emergency surgery is for incarcerated or strangulated hernias. This one has never been stuck or red and is easily reducible, so an elective repair soon is appropriate.

mmlu-professional_medicine-083.why: Recent amoxicillin, vulvovaginal redness, and a thick white discharge with a normal pH (about 4) point to vulvovaginal candidiasis. Antibiotics kill off the protective lactobacilli, and the normal pH separates candida from bacterial vaginosis and trichomonas.
notes: Bacterial vaginosis gives a thin grey fishy discharge with pH above 4.5 and little redness, not a thick white discharge at pH 4.
Chlamydia usually causes cervicitis or urethritis with mucopurulent cervical discharge, not vulvovaginal redness with a thick white discharge.
E. coli causes cystitis with dysuria. It wouldn't cause vulvovaginal redness and a thick white vaginal discharge.

mmlu-professional_medicine-086.why: Wide, fixed splitting of S2 is the hallmark of an atrial septal defect. Increased flow across the pulmonary valve gives a systolic ejection murmur at the upper left sternal border, and increased tricuspid flow gives a mid-diastolic rumble at the lower left sternal border.
notes: Aortic stenosis gives a harsh ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids, often with a click, and does not cause fixed splitting of S2.
Coarctation causes upper-limb hypertension, weak or delayed femoral pulses and a murmur heard in the back, none of which is described here.
Mitral valve prolapse gives a midsystolic click and a late systolic murmur at the apex, not fixed S2 splitting or a tricuspid flow rumble.

mmlu-professional_medicine-088.why: A new morning headache with bilateral blurred optic disc margins (papilloedema) suggests raised intracranial pressure from a mass lesion until proven otherwise. Urgent neuroimaging is needed before attributing the headache to stress or tension.
notes: Treating it as a primary headache with a beta-blocker ignores the papilloedema, a red flag that needs imaging to exclude a space-occupying lesion.
EEG assesses seizures and does not detect a cause of raised intracranial pressure, so it would not explain the papilloedema.
Referral may follow, but papilloedema calls for urgent imaging now, not a delay waiting for a specialist appointment.

mmlu-professional_medicine-095.why: A cool, pale, pulseless foot soon after a fem-pop bypass, with a weak popliteal pulse, means acute graft thrombosis or occlusion. That threatens the limb and needs prompt return to theatre for angiography and thrombectomy or revision of the graft.
notes: Compartment syndrome causes pain on passive stretch with a tense compartment, and pulses are often kept. A pulseless pale foot after bypass points to arterial occlusion.
Doppler would only confirm what the exam already shows and would delay definitive revascularisation of a threatened limb.
Thrombolysis is relatively contraindicated 2 days after major vascular surgery because of bleeding risk, and early graft failure is usually a technical problem that needs surgical correction.

mmlu-professional_medicine-099.why: Loud snoring, witnessed choking or gasping, daytime sleepiness, obesity and hypertension strongly suggest obstructive sleep apnoea. Overnight polysomnography is the diagnostic gold standard (home sleep testing is also used in Australia for high-probability cases).
notes: Ambulatory ECG looks for arrhythmias and cannot diagnose sleep-disordered breathing as the cause of daytime sleepiness.
The multiple sleep latency test is used to diagnose narcolepsy, usually after OSA has been excluded on polysomnography, and it does not measure apnoeas.
Head CT has no role here because the neurological exam is normal and the history points to sleep apnoea rather than a structural brain lesion.

mmlu-professional_medicine-111.why: Progressive symmetric proximal muscle weakness with tenderness, raised CK and LDH, joint pain, low-grade fever and cracked fingertips (mechanic's hands, typical of antisynthetase syndrome) indicate an inflammatory myopathy such as polymyositis.
notes: Fibromyalgia causes widespread pain with tender points but no objective weakness and a normal CK.
Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable weakness, often ocular or bulbar, with a normal CK and no muscle tenderness.
Scleroderma causes skin thickening, Raynaud's and sclerodactyly. Myositis can overlap with it, but marked proximal weakness with raised CK and mechanic's hands fits polymyositis better.

mmlu-professional_medicine-116.why: Numbness around the mouth and tingling fingertips 12 hours after total thyroidectomy mean hypocalcaemia from parathyroid injury or removal. Tapping the facial nerve will likely bring out a Chvostek sign, which shows the neuromuscular irritability.
notes: A bilateral Babinski sign means an upper motor neuron lesion, not hypocalcaemia after thyroidectomy.
Tongue deviation would mean hypoglossal nerve injury, which wouldn't cause numbness around the mouth or tingling fingertips.
A drooping shoulder means spinal accessory nerve injury from the neck node dissection. It doesn't explain these sensory symptoms of hypocalcaemia.

mmlu-professional_medicine-120.why: She has decision-making capacity: she understands her condition, appreciates the consequences, reasons consistently and is not depressed. A competent adult may refuse life-sustaining treatment, so keep offering insulin, respect her refusal, and provide supportive or palliative care.
notes: She has not asked to leave, and refusing one treatment does not mean ending care. Discharging her against medical advice would abandon her instead of supporting her choice.
A guardian is only needed when a patient lacks capacity. Her capacity is clearly intact, so a court order is not justified.
Nothing suggests depression or another psychiatric illness. A reasoned refusal of treatment by a competent patient is not grounds for psychiatric admission.

mmlu-professional_medicine-121.why: Fever, pharyngitis and conjunctivitis in an outbreak linked to a summer swimming pool is pharyngoconjunctival fever. The classic cause is adenovirus, which spreads through poorly chlorinated pool water and close contact.
notes: Cytomegalovirus in a healthy child usually causes a mild mononucleosis-like illness. It does not cause outbreaks of conjunctivitis with pharyngitis.
Epstein-Barr virus causes mononucleosis: exudative pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly over weeks. Conjunctivitis is not prominent and outbreaks do not spread through pools.
Influenza is mainly seasonal in winter, with cough, myalgia and coryza. Prominent conjunctivitis tied to pool exposure in summer points elsewhere.

mmlu-professional_medicine-122.why: He has massive haematemesis and a falling level of consciousness, so he cannot protect his airway and is at high risk of aspiration. Securing the airway with intubation comes first, before endoscopy or other definitive treatment of the varices.
notes: TIPS is a rescue treatment for variceal bleeding that endoscopy and drugs fail to control; it is not the immediate step in an obtunded patient with an unprotected airway.
Vasoactive therapy such as octreotide or terlipressin is started early, but it comes after the airway is secured; vasopressin is now rarely used because of ischaemic side effects.
Urgent endoscopy is the definitive treatment, but doing it in a drowsy patient who is vomiting blood risks aspiration, so he must be intubated first.

mmlu-professional_medicine-127.why: Psychiatric care involves transference and a lasting imbalance of power, so a romantic or sexual relationship with a former psychiatric patient is considered unethical at any time. Medical students are held to the same standard. In Australia, the Medical Board code and RANZCP guidance likewise treat this as effectively never acceptable.
notes: Medical students who take part in patient care carry the same fiduciary and boundary obligations as physicians, so his trainee status does not make the relationship acceptable.
Ending the clinical relationship does not end the power imbalance and transference that come from psychiatric treatment, so discharge alone does not make dating acceptable.
Waiting periods are sometimes discussed for non-psychiatric former patients, but no amount of time makes a relationship with a former psychiatric patient appropriate.

mmlu-professional_medicine-130.why: A high-achieving teenage athlete with low weight, picky eating, constipation, a request for laxatives and a relative bradycardia suggests an eating disorder or the female athlete triad. Menstrual history, looking for amenorrhoea, is the key question to ask next.
notes: Bowel habit details are routine in a constipation workup, but they miss the more important clues to an underlying eating disorder.
Nothing in the stem suggests sexually transmitted infection. Asking about it would not explain her low weight, bradycardia or wish for laxatives.
Family history of irritable bowel syndrome does not address the red flags here: low BMI, restrictive eating and laxative-seeking.

mmlu-professional_medicine-135.why: She lay immobile for a long time and has pressure-related skin changes, a CK over 10,000 U/L, and a dipstick strongly positive for blood with only rare red cells and pigmented granular casts. This is rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria, which causes acute tubular necrosis. Treat with aggressive IV fluids.
notes: ARDS can follow opioid-induced noncardiogenic pulmonary edema or aspiration, but nothing in the stem points to lung injury, while the findings clearly point to pigment-induced kidney injury.
Cerebral edema could follow hypoxic brain injury, but her vital signs are stable and the dominant findings are muscle breakdown and myoglobinuric casts, which point to the kidney.
Cocaine can cause intracerebral haemorrhage, but its blood pressure effects are acute, and the stem's key findings (CK, pigmented casts) predict acute tubular necrosis, not haemorrhage.

mmlu-professional_medicine-138.why: Painless, flesh-coloured, sessile penile lesions that turn white with acetic acid are condylomata acuminata (HPV genital warts). Cryotherapy is an appropriate first-line ablative treatment, and in Australia topical podophyllotoxin or imiquimod are also first-line options.
notes: Acyclovir treats herpes simplex, which causes painful grouped vesicles and ulcers, not persistent acetowhite papules.
Doxycycline treats chlamydia, LGV or donovanosis. LGV usually causes inguinal lymphadenopathy, and none of these cause acetowhite warty lesions.
Penicillin treats syphilis: a single painless indurated chancre or flat, moist condylomata lata. It has no effect on HPV warts.

mmlu-professional_medicine-144.why: Brief electric-shock pains in the V2/V3 area, set off by touch, chewing and cold, with a normal neurological exam and normal imaging, are classic trigeminal neuralgia. Carbamazepine is the first-line drug.
notes: Lamotrigine is sometimes used as an add-on or second-line agent in trigeminal neuralgia, but it is not first-line and needs a slow dose increase.
Levetiracetam has little evidence in trigeminal neuralgia and is not a standard first-line treatment.
Topiramate has weak evidence here and is used for migraine prevention, not as first-line treatment for trigeminal neuralgia.

mmlu-professional_medicine-145.why: Sickle cell disease shortens red cell survival, and variant haemoglobin can interfere with some assays, so HbA1c reads falsely low. That explains an A1c of 5.4% despite home readings of 140–200 mg/dL. In haemoglobinopathies, use fructosamine or glucose monitoring instead.
notes: He is only marginally adherent and his recorded readings are high, so there is no reason to believe his true control is better than his diary shows.
Nothing suggests the meter is faulty, and the poor adherence fits the elevated readings, so replacing the meter would not resolve the discrepancy.
The A1c fits a known biological effect of his haemoglobinopathy, so repeating it would most likely give a similarly falsely low result.

mmlu-professional_medicine-150.why: Mid-puberty (Tanner 3) with small bilateral subareolar fibroglandular tissue, normal genitalia, and normal hormone levels is typical of physiological pubertal gynaecomastia. It reflects a transient oestrogen–androgen imbalance and usually resolves within 1–2 years. Management is reassurance.
notes: A Leydig cell tumour would usually cause a testicular mass and raised oestradiol, but his testes are normal and oestrogen levels are within the reference range.
Peutz–Jeghers syndrome can cause gynaecomastia through oestrogen-secreting Sertoli cell tumours, but it would also cause mucocutaneous pigmentation and hamartomatous polyps, which he does not have.
Klinefelter syndrome causes small firm testes, high gonadotropins, low testosterone, and often tall stature, none of which fit his normal testes, hormone levels, and 50th-centile height.

mmlu-professional_medicine-151.why: This is acute nonspecific mechanical low back pain with no red flags: no bowel or bladder changes, normal vital signs, and a negative straight-leg raise. Staying active speeds recovery, and imaging is not indicated. Australian guidelines also recommend reassurance and staying active.
notes: Bed rest delays recovery and leads to deconditioning, so it is no longer recommended for acute low back pain.
Plain films are not indicated for acute low back pain without red flags such as trauma, older age, cancer, fever, or neurological deficit, and none is present here.
MRI is reserved for red flags or persistent radicular symptoms after conservative treatment, and this patient has neither.

mmlu-professional_medicine-153.why: Thickened, hardened skin on the hands and forearms, an expressionless face, and limited mouth opening (microstomia) suggest systemic sclerosis. Before surgery it needs evaluation because of the risk of difficult intubation and possible pulmonary, cardiac, renal, and oesophageal involvement.
notes: The masked face and flexed posture mimic parkinsonism, but muscle tone is normal (no rigidity), there is no tremor, and the skin changes point to scleroderma. The grandmother's Parkinson disease is a distractor.
Progressive supranuclear palsy causes vertical gaze palsy, early falls, and axial rigidity, none of which are described, and it would not explain the skin thickening.
Sarcopenia means loss of muscle mass and strength, but her strength is normal and it would not explain the skin hardening or microstomia.

mmlu-professional_medicine-156.why: The baby is late preterm, was born by caesarean, and has mild tachypnoea and retractions with good saturations. The X-ray shows prominent vascular markings and fluid in the fissures. This is the classic picture of transient tachypnoea of the newborn, caused by delayed clearance of lung fluid.
notes: GBS sepsis is unlikely: the baby has a normal temperature, is well, has Apgars of 9 and 9, and the X-ray shows fissural fluid rather than patchy infiltrates.
Meconium aspiration gives coarse patchy infiltrates and hyperinflation, usually in a depressed infant; light meconium staining with fissural fluid on X-ray points away from it.

Respiratory distress syndrome shows ground-glass reticulogranular lungs with air bronchograms and is more common in earlier preterm babies; at 36 weeks with fluid in the fissures, it is not the best fit.

mmlu-professional_medicine-174.why: Joint hypermobility, tall stature, myopia, a midsystolic click (mitral valve prolapse), exertional chest pain and a cousin who died of aortic rupture suggest a heritable connective tissue disorder (Marfan or Ehlers-Danlos type). Echocardiography is the key test because it assesses the aortic root and valves, which carry the life-threatening risk.
notes: A skeletal survey looks for occult fractures in suspected abuse; here the injuries are explained by hypermobility and the family history.
A bone scan detects stress fractures, infection or tumour; it does not address the possible aortic or valvular disease that matters most here.
Shoulder MRI is irrelevant to this child: the rotator cuff injury was her brother's, and her pressing issue is cardiovascular.

mmlu-professional_medicine-175.why: Postprandial epigastric and RUQ pain radiating to the right scapula after a fatty meal, in an obese 42-year-old woman, is biliary colic. RUQ ultrasound is the first-line test for gallstones: it is sensitive, non-invasive and cheap.
notes: A barium upper GI series looks at the mucosa and lumen of the stomach and small bowel; it cannot see gallstones and does not fit biliary-type pain.
CT is less sensitive than ultrasound for gallstones and exposes her to radiation; it is reserved for complications or unclear cases.
ERCP is an invasive therapeutic procedure for proven bile duct stones or obstruction; nothing here (no jaundice or abnormal LFTs) points to choledocholithiasis.

mmlu-professional_medicine-178.why: The patient has capacity, stated her wishes clearly and recorded them in her advance directive: she wants no intubation and wants to die at home. The daughter cannot override a competent patient's wishes. Arranging home hospice respects her autonomy and gives palliation and support to the family.
notes: Admitting her against her competent, documented wishes would ignore her autonomy, and the daughter has no authority to override her.
An ethics consult is not needed: the patient has capacity and a clear directive, so there is no real dilemma to resolve, and the delay would not help her comfort.
Home CPAP does not match her goal of comfort-focused care at home, and it does not address end-of-life support.

mmlu-professional_medicine-179.why: Symptoms lasting more than 7 to 10 days, purulent discharge, fever and unilateral maxillary tenderness point to acute bacterial rhinosinusitis. Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause, ahead of non-typeable H. influenzae and Moraxella.
notes: Sinusitis is caused by non-typeable H. influenzae, not type b, and even non-typeable strains come second to pneumococcus.
Moraxella catarrhalis is a recognised but less common cause, seen more often in children.
Staphylococcus aureus is uncommon in community-acquired acute sinusitis and is more typical of chronic or nosocomial sinusitis.

mmlu-professional_medicine-180.why: Green (bilious or enteric) fluid from a chest tube, together with loss of the diaphragm shadow, means a ruptured diaphragm with injured, herniated bowel. In a hypotensive patient this calls for immediate laparotomy. Unstable patients go to theatre, not to the CT scanner.
notes: Abdominal CT is for haemodynamically stable patients. She is in shock with clear evidence of hollow-viscus injury.
Chest CT would delay definitive repair in an unstable patient, and the diagnosis is already evident.
Thoracoscopy can assess the diaphragm in stable patients, but it cannot deal with bowel injury and should not be done in shock.

mmlu-professional_medicine-186.why: Periorbital and generalised oedema, ascites and weight gain with no JVP rise or heart failure signs suggest nephrotic syndrome. Regular high-dose ibuprofen is a likely cause, through minimal change disease or membranous nephropathy, so urine protein will be markedly raised.
notes: She has no risk factors for HIV (monogamous, no IV drug use), and nothing points to HIV-associated nephropathy.
There is no JVP rise, no gallop and the lungs are clear, so heart failure is unlikely and BNP should be normal.
Her brief cocaine use was 16 years ago and would not explain a nephrotic picture now.

mmlu-professional_medicine-196.why: Petechiae, meningism and gram-negative diplococci in the CSF indicate meningococcal meningitis. A third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone is the treatment of choice. In Australia, benzylpenicillin is often given before arrival in hospital, and contacts need clearance and prophylaxis.
notes: Clindamycin does not reach the CSF well enough and does not cover Neisseria meningitidis.
Erythromycin penetrates the CSF poorly and is not used for bacterial meningitis.
Metronidazole covers anaerobes, such as in brain abscess, not meningococcus.

mmlu-professional_medicine-203.why: A hot, swollen, red knee with fever and limited movement is septic arthritis until proven otherwise. Aspirate the joint (Gram stain, culture, cell count) before starting antibiotics so the organism can be identified.
notes: A nuclear scan is slow and nonspecific, and it does not provide fluid for diagnosis.
MRI delays diagnosis. Synovial fluid analysis is the key test.
Antibiotics are needed urgently, but starting them before aspiration lowers the culture yield. Aspirate first.

mmlu-professional_medicine-208.why: The bullet passed through the abdomen into the left chest, and breath sounds are reduced on that side in a hypotensive patient. That suggests haemothorax or pneumothorax. Under ATLS order, breathing problems are treated first with a left chest tube, and then laparotomy follows.
notes: CT is not appropriate in an unstable patient with penetrating trauma.
Positive-pressure ventilation before draining a possible pneumothorax could turn it into a tension pneumothorax. He is also maintaining his own airway.
Peritoneal lavage is unnecessary. A penetrating thoracoabdominal wound with shock needs surgery, and the chest has to be decompressed first.

mmlu-professional_medicine-214.why: Tall stature, sparse facial hair, gynaecomastia, small firm testes and azoospermia are classic Klinefelter syndrome. A karyotype showing 47,XXY confirms the underlying cause.
notes: Low testosterone and raised oestradiol fit the picture but do not show the chromosomal cause.
Raised FSH and LH show primary testicular failure but cannot tell you why it occurred.
High prolactin causes hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, not small firm testes with this body habitus.

mmlu-professional_medicine-222.why: She has non-purulent cellulitis after a scrape and has had anaphylaxis to penicillin, so beta-lactams should be avoided. Clindamycin covers streptococci and staphylococci and is the standard alternative. This matches Australian Therapeutic Guidelines for immediate severe penicillin allergy.
notes: Amoxicillin is a penicillin and is contraindicated after anaphylaxis; it also covers staphylococci poorly.
Ciprofloxacin has poor streptococcal coverage and is not a suitable choice for simple cellulitis.
Clarithromycin is a macrolide; her rash with erythromycin makes it a poor choice, and streptococcal resistance to macrolides is common.

mmlu-professional_medicine-223.why: She has recurrent episodes of spinning vertigo lasting hours, with fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus and fullness in the same ear. Together these make up the classic picture of Meniere's disease (endolymphatic hydrops). Remember the four features: episodic vertigo, low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness.
notes: Acoustic neuroma usually causes slowly progressive one-sided hearing loss and tinnitus with mild imbalance, not discrete 12-hour attacks of vertigo with aural fullness.
In benign positional vertigo, attacks last seconds, are triggered by head position and do not affect hearing.

Brainstem TIAs last minutes and cause other brainstem signs such as diplopia, dysarthria or weakness. They are unlikely in a healthy 35-year-old and do not explain repeated attacks in one ear with aural fullness.

mmlu-professional_medicine-224.why: Several findings point to a peritonsillar abscess: one-sided swelling of the soft palate, the uvula pushed to the other side, trismus and a muffled 'hot potato' voice. The abscess needs drainage, either by needle aspiration or by incision and drainage, as well as antibiotics.
notes: Corticosteroids are sometimes given alongside treatment to ease symptoms, but they do not replace draining the abscess.
Nystatin treats oral candidiasis, which would not cause a febrile, one-sided peritonsillar swelling with trismus.
Salt water gargles only ease symptoms and do nothing for an abscess that needs drainage.

mmlu-professional_medicine-230.why: Sharing a room with someone who has meningococcal disease makes her a close contact. She needs chemoprophylaxis to clear carriage, and rifampin is the listed choice. In Australia, a single dose of ciprofloxacin is usually preferred, with rifampicin or ceftriaxone as alternatives.
notes: Vaccination may also be offered, but it does not protect her immediately and does not replace chemoprophylaxis.
Doxycycline is not used to clear meningococcal carriage.
Penicillin treats invasive disease but does not reliably clear carriage from the nasopharynx, so it is not used for prophylaxis.

mmlu-professional_medicine-236.why: For 2 months he has had a reduced need for sleep, increased energy and goal-directed activity, distractibility, rapid speech and a labile affect. These fit a manic episode, which means bipolar disorder. He has been off substances for 3 years, so they do not explain it.
notes: Antisocial personality disorder is a lifelong pattern of disregarding others' rights. It does not explain a new 2-month change in sleep, energy and mood.
ADHD must start in childhood. He did well in school, and his symptoms appeared only recently, along with a reduced need for sleep.
Borderline personality disorder involves long-standing unstable relationships, fear of abandonment and self-harm, not a distinct episode of elevated mood with little need for sleep.

mmlu-professional_medicine-237.why: Orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, raised JVP, crackles, an S3 and oedema all indicate heart failure, and the apical holosystolic murmur radiating to the axilla suggests mitral regurgitation. Echocardiography confirms both by showing ventricular function and the valve abnormality.
notes: Troponin is used to look for myocardial injury in suspected acute coronary syndrome. She has no chest pain, and troponin cannot show valve or ventricular structure.
An ECG may show nonspecific changes but cannot confirm heart failure or mitral regurgitation.
A stress test looks for inducible ischaemia. It does not diagnose valve disease and is unsafe in decompensated heart failure.

mmlu-professional_medicine-241.why: An antipsychotic was recently started, and he now has fever, muscle rigidity, autonomic instability (tachycardia, hypertension, sweating), fluctuating consciousness, raised CK and leukocytosis. This is the classic picture of neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
notes: Amphetamine intoxication causes agitation, a fast pulse and dilated pupils, but marked rigidity with altered consciousness after a new antipsychotic fits NMS better.
Bacterial meningitis is less likely because his neck is supple, and it would not explain the generalised rigidity and raised CK after a new antipsychotic.
Delirium tremens occurs 2 to 4 days after stopping alcohol and features tremor and hallucinations, not lead-pipe rigidity. Nothing in the stem suggests recent alcohol withdrawal.

mmlu-professional_medicine-243.why: Total knee replacement carries a high risk of venous thromboembolism, and subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin is effective standard prophylaxis that needs no monitoring. In Australia, oral apixaban or rivaroxaban is also commonly used after knee replacement.
notes: Pneumatic compression alone protects less well than drug prophylaxis after knee replacement. It is mainly used when anticoagulation is contraindicated or alongside drugs.
A titrated heparin infusion is a treatment dose that raises bleeding risk and needs monitoring. It is not prophylaxis.
Warfarin takes days to work, needs INR monitoring and interacts with many drugs, so it is less suitable than enoxaparin in this setting.

mmlu-professional_medicine-245.why: The mother is your patient's guardian and the only legitimate route to the father. The best first step is to address her anger and explain how knowing the father's carrier status helps her son (recurrence risk, prognosis) and the father's relatives. Confidentiality and consent mean you work through the family, not around them.
notes: Going to the father's physician behind the mother's back breaches confidentiality about the child, and you have not yet tried to get the mother on side.
Phoning the father directly discloses the child's genetic information without the guardian's consent and skips the step of working with the mother.
Giving up too early leaves the child and family without useful information; you should first try to engage and educate the mother.

mmlu-professional_medicine-256.why: Acute urticaria (under 6 weeks) in a patient with a normal history and examination is usually self-limited and idiopathic or due to a viral trigger. No investigations are needed, so treat the symptoms with a non-sedating H1 antihistamine.
notes: Serum IgE is nonspecific and does not change management of a first, self-limited episode with no abnormal findings.
An eosinophil count adds nothing when history and examination are normal and there are no clues to parasitic or systemic disease.
Specialist referral is for chronic urticaria or features of anaphylaxis, not a first, brief episode that has settled.

mmlu-professional_medicine-257.why: A heavy smoker with a hilar mass (probable small cell carcinoma), proximal leg weakness, absent reflexes, mild ptosis, and dry mouth and eyes has Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome. Antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels reduce acetylcholine release.
notes: Myopathy causes proximal weakness, but reflexes are usually kept and it does not explain the autonomic dry mouth and eyes or the ptosis.
The dryness is autonomic, but the underlying problem is reduced presynaptic acetylcholine release at both nicotinic and muscarinic synapses, not a primary parasympathetic lesion.
Peripheral neuropathy would usually cause distal weakness with sensory loss, but sensation here is normal.

mmlu-professional_medicine-263.why: A teenager who tells you about groin lumps only after his mother leaves suggests inguinal lymphadenopathy that could come from a sexually transmitted infection. A confidential sexual history (HEADSS approach) is the key next step.
notes: Systemic symptoms matter, but the private disclosure of groin lumps points first to a sexual history to look for an STI.
He seems sullen, but mood questions do not explain or address the groin lumps he raised in private.
School performance is part of a psychosocial screen, but it does not help you assess new inguinal lumps.

mmlu-professional_medicine-264.why: A raised MSAFP should first be followed by ultrasound. The commonest cause is wrong dating, and her dates are uncertain here. Ultrasound also detects multiple pregnancy, fetal death, and neural tube or abdominal wall defects.
notes: Repeating MSAFP delays diagnosis and does not resolve uncertain dates or detect structural defects.
Triple screening is mainly for aneuploidy risk; it adds little once MSAFP is already clearly raised and the dating is uncertain.
Amniocentesis is invasive and only considered if ultrasound confirms the dates and shows no explanation; it is not the first step.

mmlu-professional_medicine-269.why: She has major depression with anxiety features and probable nocturnal panic attacks: low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep and concentration, and suicidal ideation without a plan. An SSRI such as paroxetine is first-line. Her ferritin is normal, so iron deficiency is not the cause.
notes: Her memory lapses come from depression (pseudodementia), not Alzheimer disease, so a cholinesterase inhibitor is not indicated.
A ferritin of 140 ng/mL rules out iron deficiency, so iron would not help her mild anaemia or her mood.
Ginkgo has no proven benefit for depression or cognition and would delay effective treatment.

mmlu-professional_medicine-270.why: A sharp, long object (a 4 cm nail) that is still in the stomach, within reach of the scope, should be removed endoscopically. Once it passes the pylorus it can perforate the bowel. The rule to remember: remove sharp objects and objects longer than about 5-6 cm before they leave the stomach.
notes: Ipecac is no longer recommended, and forcing a sharp object back up by vomiting risks injury to the oesophagus and aspiration.
Waiting for it to pass suits small blunt objects, but a sharp nail carries a high risk of perforating the bowel as it moves through.
There is no free air and the patient is stable, so surgery is not needed while a less invasive endoscopic removal is possible.

mmlu-professional_medicine-271.why: Exertional chest pain radiating to the jaw, now recurring, is suspected acute coronary syndrome. Immediate relief comes from a nitrate such as sublingual GTN, which releases nitric oxide, raises cGMP and causes venodilation, lowering preload and myocardial oxygen demand.
notes: Drugs that raise cAMP, such as dobutamine or milrinone, increase myocardial contractility and oxygen demand, which would worsen ischaemia.
Potassium channel blockers such as amiodarone are class III antiarrhythmics; he is in sinus rhythm at 80/min and has no arrhythmia to treat.
Sodium channel blockers such as lidocaine are class I antiarrhythmics; they do not relieve ischaemic chest pain and are not used routinely in ACS.

headqa-2014-111.why: review: The gout note says allopurinol is 'never' started during an acute attack, which is outdated: current guidance allows starting urate-lowering therapy during a flare with anti-inflammatory or colchicine cover.
